#5777. China Truck Sales Now Majority Electric. What’s Next?

EV heavy trucks hit 50.3% market share in China for September, with sales up 34% from a year ago. Long-haul big rig market share hit 64.5%. China is on track to have over 40% EV market share for the entire year, reaching their 2030 goal in a matter of months. This is not the first time China’s heavy truck market share topped 50%, but that previous blip in December last year was prior to subsidies ending, followed by a dip in January. Current sales rates are not bolstered by the subsidy and are now on a much more stable upward trajectory.

The speed of EV adoption for heavy trucks in China has recently grown much faster than for cars, having risen from just 13.6% in 2024. When I visited Guangzhou in November of last year and again in April of this year, I noticed a lot more green plates on trucks, indicating that they were electric. It seems that my perception is backed by sales data.

With the addition of LNG trucks, diesel’s share of heavy trucks has dropped to roughly 40%. While LNG sales have also declined with the rate of EV adoption, diesel trucks could soon make up less than 1/3 of sales and decline further from there. China could feasibly double its 2030 goal and hit 80% EV penetration, by which point many diesel models are likely to be discontinued.

With these levels of market penetration, in addition to retirements, China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, despite increased freight movement. Every additional electric truck that replaces a diesel truck then builds on that reduction. Due to their duty cycle, each electric truck sold has a much greater impact on fuel consumption than each car sold. And the price of fuel combined with the duty cycle has a much greater impact on overall truck economics.

To be clear, these improving results are not due to subsidies, as they appear in the year after subsidies were cut. They are also not due to mandates, as the 2030 goals were met before the ink was dry on their announcement. EV trucks are now more affordable to own and operate than diesel trucks in China. The increase in diesel prices has only increased the cost gap.

Last year, roughly 90% of all electric truck sales globally were in China. That percentage is set to expand this year, despite rising sales in some other countries. Those sales are simply not rising fast enough outside of China to keep pace with China. In comparison, the EU is looking at 2.5% EV market share this year. China is on pace to average roughly as many electric trucks sold per week as Europe sells per year. The US EV truck market looks like a rounding error in comparison at less than one percent.

In addition, China has rapidly been building out heavy truck charging infrastructure as part of the 28 million charging facilities planned to be in operation by the end of 2027, up from 21 million last March. This not only focuses on the major cities but also extends into more rural areas that have been slower to adopt electrification. In addition, several companies are building out battery swap stations. While we have yet to see if battery swap or MW+ charging wins in the truck market, expect the competition between the two approaches to be fierce.

Within Tier 1 cities, I could see a potential phase out of diesel trucks in the near future. Hainan province is already planning to end ICE passenger car sales by 2030, and I expect that to extend to diesel trucks as well. Although rural areas have been slower to adopt, they also tend to be less wealthy and thus more impacted by the changing economics. If diesel prices stay elevated while charging becomes convenient, many rural businesses will not be able to afford to buy new diesel trucks. With the end of diesel truck sales, strict emissions standards and a potential return of scrappage incentives could take remaining diesel vehicles off the road at an accelerated rate.

With fewer diesel trucks on the road in the largest market globally, diesel consumption is set to decline. In addition, the supply chain for diesel parts will also start to decline. As protectionism has targeted electric vehicles, rather than internal combustion  engine (ICE) vehicles, a decline in Chinese (ICE) parts has a potentially significant impact on global markets.

Of course, as EVs take over the majority of heavy truck sales in the fiercely competitive Chinese market, Chinese manufacturers will start looking outside of the country for growth.

The traditional thought would be to look at wealthy Western countries that have substantial buying power. However, many Chinese companies may be a bit reluctant to focus on those markets after the protectionist efforts against electric passenger vehicles. Many European markets, like Germany, also have very high electricity prices, which makes the financial proposition less attractive for commercial vehicles that are heavily motivated by costs. Chinese companies may start focusing elsewhere.

The Middle Corridor could become a focus. This essentially rebuilds the Silk Road land route from China, across the Caspian Sea, on to Turkey. Many of the countries along this route  once had prosperous trade, only to fall into decline when ocean trade routes were established. However, land transport is much easier to electrify than long ocean voyages. China is investing heavily with countries like Kazakhstan along the route with renewable electricity infrastructure. Electrified rail is expanding by 26-fold in Turkey. Electrified trucking is the next logical step, connecting the rail lines to more local production along the route.

Other Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) countries could also benefit. In countries like Ethiopia, which has expensive diesel but electricity prices to businesses of just $0.017/kWh, electric trucks could make perfect sense to transport between new factories and new ports. Trading partners like Vietnam and Thailand could also see an influx.

All this is not to say that local companies will not benefit. Unlike passenger cars, heavy equipment tends to be more modular. Due to the bulk and mass of the vehicles, final assembly is more likely to be localized, with greater use of local suppliers.

Overall, we could see much of the “Rest of the World” (ROW) leapfrog legacy economies in EV truck adoption. The purchase price is no longer prohibitive in China, and the operating costs are much lower. With infrastructure buildout and increasing renewable installed capacity, electric trucking is poised to take over rapidly.

That is not to say that the West will be completely left out. Countries with less prohibitive trade policies toward EVs will likely see increased adoption. While EVs have taken over passenger car sales in Norway, their trucking industry still has a way to go at just 14.4%. And the geographically most eastern country typically lumped in with the “West,” Australia, is likely to see EV truck sales follow a similar pattern to EV car sales. If Canada continues to open up, they could also benefit. Of course, as the majority of the economic benefit from electric trucks comes from their use, inflated trucking costs hurt every company that moves products by truck, and those inflated costs then lead to inflation throughout the economy. That impacts overall affordability. As such, there is a chance that protectionists do not put as much effort into undermining electric truck imports as they put into passenger EVs.

And the EV heavy truck global supply chain will become increasingly well established. This could mean more parts availability for brands outside of China to build competitive vehicles, if those companies have access to global supply chains. Competitive markets will also drive innovation, moving the technology forward at an accelerating rate. Meanwhile the supply chain for diesel trucks will shrink.

While the US still seems to be figuring out how to make a safe EV Semi, battery-powered heavy trucks are becoming increasingly mature products elsewhere. As electric trucks move from majority share to complete market dominance in the largest market, other markets will follow, and the transition will become inevitable. Hopefully, the largest oil producing country in the world will not be left too far behind.

#5776. APS expects sales to double by 2041, plans extending coal use to 2038

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Peak demand will grow about 3.4% annually over the next 15 years, driven by industry and data centers, Arizona Public Service said in an integrated resource plan filed Friday with regulators.

APS projects peak demand of more than 14.5 GW in 2041, almost 60% higher than its current record peak of about 9.2 GW, set in August. And the utility expects annual retail sales to grow to about 80,600 GWh in 2041, up from about 34,200 GWh in 2025.

There is some uncertainty behind APS’ load projections, but the utility said it has taken steps to protect customers.

Despite refinements to APS’ large-load interconnection process, the “sustained record levels of interest” from large customers poses “a risk in increased potential for unrealized loads,” APS said in its resource plan, which it files every three years with the Arizona Corporation Commission. To mitigate the risk, APS said it adopted strategies such as having customers commit to “minimum demand and energy-based contract terms, providing collateral in case of default, and instituting early exit fees.”

As a result of population growth and higher levels of economic activity, APS said it expects to add up to 29,000 residential customers annually in the near term, and across the planning period the utility anticipates annual customer growth to be in the range of 1.5% to 2.5% through 2030.

The utility’s preferred plan includes continuing to operate the Four Corners coal plant beyond a planned 2031 retirement. APS said the extension could save customers close to $1 billion.

“The company will continue to evaluate the appropriate time to cease operations between 2031 and 2038, with the decision depending on customer needs, economics and other factors evaluated through future planning processes,” APS said in a statement.

“Reliability is nonnegotiable,” Mike Eugenis, APS director of resource planning, said in a statement.

APS’ planned natural gas resource additions include repowering the Cholla Power Plant as a 387-MW facility by 2030, adding 1,107 MW through new combustion turbines at existing APS sites and uprates to tolling units during 2026-2030, according to the IRP. Under the plan, APS will also add the 1,238 MW Desert Sun combined-cycle facility in 2032 to serve large-customer subscription load.

Customer and clean energy advocates were critical of the APS plan.

APS’ proposal “further delays our move from gas and coal to solar and wind,” Sierra Club Grand Canyon Chapter Director Sandy Bahr said in a statement. “We’re seeing these utilities protect their own bottom lines, instead of making the most economical decisions for ratepayers.”

The utility “should be investing in proven community-based energy solutions, like local solar and battery storage,” Vote Solar West Senior Regulatory Director Kate Bowman said in a statement.

APS “failed to consider how alternative technologies like rooftop solar, battery storage, and other distributed resources could help meet energy needs,” Bowman said. As the ACC considers the plan, regulators will have “an opportunity to push for a more comprehensive approach that puts affordability, reliability, and the interests of customers at the center of long-term planning,” she added.

The utility said it is adding nearly 2 GW of renewable utility-scale solar and 2.5 GW of battery storage in the next two years, “diversifying our resources to keep energy reliable and affordable.” By 2030, APS said it expects to have approximately 6 GW of battery storage on its system.

The utility also expects continued growth in customer-sited resources. APS said behind-the-meter storage adoption is expected to grow every year to 1.2 GW by 2045 — up from 69 MW today. For 2032, the storage forecast is approximately 95% higher compared to the last storage forecast developed in 2023, APS said.

Behind-the-meter solar adoption is expected to slow relative to the 2020-2023 period but “will still experience some modest growth,” reaching 3.7 GW by 2045 — up from 2.1 GW today.

Electric vehicles in APS service territory are expected to grow from 65,000 vehicles today to 1.1 million in 2045, resulting in 5.2 TWh of EV charging load, APS said. In 2042, this forecast is approximately 18% lower compared to the last EV forecast developed in 2023, it noted.

#5775. How Does Oahu Get to an Economically Resilient, 100% Clean Energy Future?

Oahu is a unique place. It’s the home of one of the largest clean tech incubators in the world, Elemental Impact, for a reason. Exorbitantly high electricity rates combined with ample natural resources make it an incredible laboratory to bring clean tech solutions to market. Rapid investment for WWII created a grid that was dependent on foreign oil. Path dependency (the idea that “what you know” becomes what you continue to do) hampered innovation and resulted in the creation of infrastructure (multiple power plants across multiple islands) that still, today, burns diesel fuel as large generators, to produce electricity for the island. Throw in a dependence on imported fuels that must come at least 3,000 miles to arrive, being the strategic hub for the entire Pacific theater of the U.S. military, one of the wildest weather years and hurricane seasons the island chain has ever seen AND the state’s economic dependency on tourism dollars, high cost of living, and low wages, and and wow – you’ve got yourself a puzzle and a half to solve in order to get the place to a sustainable future.

Analyst Mike Barnard loves a challenge, so he set forth to put together a roadmap to help Oahu get to 100% clean energy, which helps recirculate money in the state, lower costs, create jobs and foster economic resiliency.

Recently I gave a talk at Hawaii Tech Week in which I summarized this report, added in my own experience running an energy efficiency service that has now greened more than 20,000 homes and is saving Hawaii residents over $10 million a year on their utility bills, and then compiled the new and coming technologies that can help the island get off fossil fuels.

Mike’s report did something very important. The state’s own reporting and strategy looks at the big picture, a very difficult mountain to climb. Mike looked at that mountain and removed some of the false summits and unachievable viewpoints, resulting in a much more achievable and strategic pathway. What he did was eliminate the things we simply cannot fix right now – long distance flights, maritime bunkering, and military fuels – and tackled the problem of Oahu’s actual energy consumption for its residents. The result was that it was achievable, and there are technologies right now today that can be deployed in what he refers to as a “no regret stack” first and foremost.

I combined that with my approach, which was to showcase the economic resilience it creates. Case in point, an LED bulb saves so much money on Oahu that it pays for itself in 18 days. Every day after that, it is like change plinking in a piggy bank for the person who put it in. That builds economic resiliency for those who need it most. From LEDs to e-bikes to heat pump water heaters to balcony solar – it all adds up – fast payback periods, and financial independence.

Mike comes back to the things we simply can’t fix right now and argues that the tech will come – but for the duration of the 2020s and into the 2030s, we should be installing parking lot solar canopies, agrivoltaics, heat pump water heaters, and more.

Scott Cooney (LinkedIn) is a serial eco-entrepreneur focused on making the world a better place for all its residents. Scott is the founder of CleanTechnica and was just smart enough to hire someone smarter than him to run it. He then started Pono Home, a service that greens homes, which has performed efficiency retrofits on more than 20,000 homes and small businesses, reducing carbon pollution by more than 27 million pounds a year and saving customers more than $6.3 million a year on their utilities. Scott wanted to contribute to native ownership of the clean energy revolution, so he gifted Pono Home to a long tenured employee with native Hawaiian roots for just the liquidation value, turning down a mainland company interested in purchasing the company. In a previous life, Scott was an adjunct professor of Sustainability in the MBA program at the University of Hawai'i, a consultant at Saatchi & Saatchi S, where he worked with a team to educate and empower millions of employees to live healthier and more sustainably. He is the author of Build a Green Small Business: Profitable Ways to Become an Ecopreneur (McGraw-Hill) , and Green Living Ideas. Scott is an occasional investor, currently he has investments in Rivian (RIVN).

#5774. Mid-Air Helicopter Collision Near Everest Base Camp Kills Tourist, Injures 2 Others

Although an entire tourism industry has grown around climbing Mount Everest, summiting the world's tallest mountain remains a tremendously dangerous endeavor. Two helicopters collided in mid-air while attempting to land at the same spot below the Everest base camp. Helicopter company Fishtail Air stated that the crash killed an Indian tourist, and the chopper's captain and another passenger were injured. The other helicopter's pilot somehow escaped without injury. The second chopper was only carrying cargo.

The footage is harrowing, to say the least. A red helicopter is hovering, gradually descending and rotating to a landing spot at Pheriche. The Nepali village sits 13,780 feet above sea level. Then, a second helicopter comes into frame, seemingly appearing out of nowhere. Both pilots take evasive action far too late. The second chopper's main blades smash into the other rotorcraft, slicing off the tail boom. Both helicopters immediately plummet right into the snowy terrain as people waiting on the ground scramble away. Miraculously, none of the bystanders were struck by flying debris or injured. There's never a good outcome when two helicopters hit each other.

It's pretty baffling how two helicopters could collide in completely clear conditions. Maybe the pilots didn't realize they were trying to land in the same spot. Helicopter flights aren't rare in this part of the world, either. According to the BBC, helicopters are the only way to get trekkers and guides down from Everest when they are sick or exhausted in inhospitable conditions. It's also the tail end of the mountain's autumn climbing season.

The tourists who spend thousands of dollars to climb Everest do so with the understanding that it's inherently dangerous. Those dangers are typically low oxygen levels and freezing temperatures at absurdly high altitudes. Just getting to the mountain can be just as dangerous. Most journeys to Everest base camp begin at Tenzing-Hillary Airport, named after the first mountaineers to climb the mountain. The facility is often called the world's most dangerous airport because of its short 1,729-foot runway with a 12% gradient and the mountain wall at one end. Not to mention, the terrain doesn't allow pilots to go around despite the rapidly shifting weather conditions. Just flying in would be enough of an Everest adventure for me.

#5773. De-Escalated Treatment for HPV-Related Throat Cancer Gets Long-Term Supporting Data

— More than 90% of patients alive without evidence of disease at 5 years

Reduced-intensity treatment for human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) led to durable cancer control in more than 90% of patients, long-term follow-up from a prospective study showed.

After a median follow-up of 5 years, 94% of patients had no evidence of disease and 90.6% were alive at last follow-up after de-escalated elective nodal irradiation (ENI) during definitive concurrent chemoradiation (CRT). Five-year locoregional control, distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS), and overall survival (OS) exceeded 90%. All but one patient with locoregional failure had recurrences in areas with known residual macroscopic disease. No treatment failures occurred in nodal basins that were omitted from treatment.

De-escalation came in the form of 30-Gy ENI instead of the usual 50-60 Gy dose and omission of low-risk nodal basins, reported Nancy Y. Lee, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, and colleagues in JAMA Oncology.

"These outcomes were attained across the spectrum of T- and N-stage groups and smoking histories among patients predominantly treated with concurrent platinum-based chemoradiosensitization," the authors noted. "The systematic omission of uninvolved nodal levels IB/V did not result in failures in those areas and provides a simple class solution to reducing irradiated volume and toxic effects. The 30-Gy ENI dose remains the lowest among published approaches, is tailored to HPV-associated disease, and results in the lowest reported gastrostomy tube insertion rate."

"Although low-dose ENI without concurrent chemotherapy has been investigated, recent phase III randomized trials have demonstrated the superiority of concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy for achieving cure in HPV-associated OPC, underscoring the importance of de-escalating ENI within an optimally curative paradigm for HPV-associated OPC," they wrote.

The study showed that focusing on radiation dose is not the only strategy to de-escalate treatment for HPV-associated OPC, said David Sher, MD, of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, who was not involved in the study.

"While we often focus on the total dose delivered to visible cancer, in actuality, ENI is responsible for a substantial amount of normal tissue irradiation and dose to critical normal structures, such as the salivary glands and swallowing structures," Sher, an expert for the American Society for Radiation Oncology, told MedPage Today. "There has been a progressive recognition that ENI dose can be a significant contributor to quality-of-life outcomes, and there are several studies, both prospective and retrospective, that have shown that the standard dose of 50 Gy can be substantially lowered."

"[The] degree of success is remarkable given the extent of dose reduction, and it is exciting to see such superb outcomes," he added. "Although we do not have quality-of-life data from this study, prior reports were also very favorable."

Providing additional context for the study results, Sher noted that all patients underwent PET-CT imaging and the vast majority had MRI as well. Such advanced imaging may play a key role in identifying smaller lymph nodes that might harbor cancer and require higher radiation doses. Additionally, all the patients received cisplatin-containing chemotherapy, and HPV-associated OPC is cisplatin sensitive. Also, the authors did not report how many "equivocal" lymph nodes were treated with a higher radiation dose.

Results of the current study add to those of a previous phase III trial that used a slightly higher nodal irradiation dose, he added.

"All of this work strongly suggests we are delivering ENI doses that are far too high, and we need to be more aggressive in reducing the acute and long-term side-effect burden of our treatments while preserving oncologic efficacy," said Sher. "For such a result to become a true standard of care, though, we do need a phase III randomized study to confirm non-inferiority in a multi-institutional setting, and hopefully such a trial can be available soon to patients and our community."

Lee and colleagues previously reported 2-year outcomes with the de-escalation strategy, showing good locoregional control and survival with "excellent" quality of life. The current report aimed to establish the durability of the strategy, as assessed after a median follow-up of 5 years.

The analysis involved 276 patients treated with intensity-modulated radiotherapy (n=256) or intensity-modulated proton therapy (n=20). Treated nodal and subclinical regions received 30 Gy in 15 fractions and a sequential boost of 40 Gy in 20 fractions.

The 5-year results showed that 260 patients had no evidence of disease at 5 years and 250 were alive at last follow-up. Five-year outcomes were:

A single elective nodal failure occurred 6 months after concurrent CRT in a contralateral indeterminate lymph node present at baseline and treated with 30 Gy, the authors reported. The last regional failure occurred 18 months post-treatment. Distant-only recurrences occurred in 23 patients. At last follow-up, 12 of the patients remained alive with no evidence of disease, and one remained alive with disease.

#5772. XPENG Sales Soar!

XPENG had a fantabulous sales month in October. We can give you the numbers, but as you can see well enough in the chart above and below, the company’s sales soared to a whole new level last month.

Reaching 50,237 vehicle deliveries, that meant 22% sales growth month over month and 20% sales growth year over year. There were 41,256 XPENG vehicles delivered in September 2026 and 42,013 delivered in October 2025, the company’s previous monthly record. Will it be another year until XPENG beats its monthly sales record again, or is the October 2026 result just the beginning of more record sales in coming months?

Oh, wait, I’ll also add that XPENG’s big spike in sales in October helped the company to shoot high above similar (but different) rival NIO in their long-term battle as the best selling smart EV startup.

#5770. Oil Companies Will Love That The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado's New V8s Get Worse Gas Mileage Than The Old Ones

Due to a litany of misguided decisions on behalf of the Trump administration, gas is ridiculously expensive right now, corporate fuel economy requirements are worryingly low, and we're in an affordability crisis. In totally unrelated news, the oil and gas companies that spent millions to elect Trump are raking in record profits that are more than double what they were at this time last year. Those oil companies are doing fine, but they will still likely be stoked to learn that GM announced the fuel economy numbers for V8-powered examples of the freshly redesigned 2027 Chevrolet Silverado today, and they all get worse gas mileage than the outgoing Silverado's V8s. These numbers should all also apply to the 2027 GMC Sierra, too.

According to documents posted by GM Authority, the fuel economy of all Silverados equipped with either the new 5.7-liter V8 or the new 6.6-liter V8 has dropped between 1 and 2 mpg across city ratings, highway ratings, and combined ratings. While these drops aren't especially significant, it's rare to see redesigned versions of cars debut with worse efficiency than their predecessors, even when we're talking about big trucks.

2027 Silverados fitted with the 5.7-liter V8 are rated at 16 mpg city, 19 mpg highway, and 17 combined in two-wheel-drive form; opting for four-wheel drive drops both the highway and combined ratings by an additional mpg. Those city and combined figures are each down one mpg, and the highway rating is down two mpg compared to the 2026 Silverado.

Trucks with the 6.6-liter V8 are only shown in four-wheel-drive, and are rated at 14 mpg in the city, 18 mpg on the highway, and 15 mpg combined. If you go for the off-road-oriented Silverado ZR2, it drops the city and combined figures by 1 mpg and the highway figure by 3 mpg. (The same should go for the Sierra's AT4X equivalent.) All of those numbers are down by either 1 or 2 mpg when compared to their fuel economy ratings in 2026.

Even opting for the 3.0-liter inline-six turbodiesel powertrain option won't save as much fuel as it did last year. Most diesel-powered 2027 Silverados return between 1 and 2 mpg worse than last year, except for city mileage in some four-wheel-drive trims. City and highway mileage for the diesel ZR2 remains the same. Mileage ratings for the turbocharged 2.7-liter four-cylinder powertrain have not been published yet.

Considering that the Chevrolet Silverado almost always lands in the second-place spot on the list of best-selling vehicles in the U.S. behind the Ford F-Series, and the GMC Sierra isn't too far behind, the impact of small changes in efficiency get magnified. So far through the third quarter of 2026, GMC sold 252,639 Sierras and Chevrolet sold 413,383 Silverados, and production of the new-gen trucks only just started in October. Though not all of these trucks will be fitted with one of the new V8s, certainly a ton of them will, and decreasing even just V8 gas mileage by a single mpg will still result in a massive increase in collective fuel usage.

#5766. At $18,000, Could This 1997 Bentley Brooklands Let You See How The Other Half Lives?

Based on today's Nice Price or No Dice Bentley's price, you don't have to be a one-percent-er to live life large. Let's see if this stately and imposing saloon makes us want to live it up.

On their third album, "Learning to Crawl," Chrissie Hynde and The Pretenders warned us of "Time the Avenger." A song about bad decisions, regret, and the inability to turn back the clock, it fit the album's tone perfectly, following the untimely deaths of two band members.

The fact is, time keeps marching forward, and we can never slow its pace or fully reverse its effects. That makes looking at cars like the 2001 Audi A4 Quattro Avant we considered yesterday such a scary proposition. While the seller promised that many of the car's wear-and-tear items had been addressed, with any old Audi, there's always some new surprise to darken a day and lighten a wallet. That expectation of future failures on this 25-year-old Audi gave pause, calling into question its $7,450 asking price. In the end, that was just too much to risk, and we saw an overwhelming 73% 'No Dice' loss as a result.

Okay, if you all had a hard time justifying the potential future costs of an old mid-level Audi, let's see how you do with today's far fancier-pantsed 1997 Bentley Brooklands saloon. Bentley offered the Brooklands for a short five years, from 1993 to 1998, though the model was merely an evolution of the earlier Mulsanne, introduced all the way back in 1980. That makes the model a grand dame of British luxury comportment.

Following the marque's fancy of naming its models after race tracks or sections thereof, the Brooklands takes its name from the Brooklands circuit outside of Surrey, England. It was the world's first banked oval raceway, inspiring the Indianapolis Motor Speedway when it opened in 1907 and hosting its last race in 1939. In the years in between, Bentleys raced on the track, reinforcing the model's legacy. In another unique connection, the British aircraft manufacturer Vickers located a factory at the Brooklands Aerodrome, right next to the track, and later, when this Brooklands was built, that company was the majority owner of Rolls-Royce and Bentley.

With that bit of history out of the way, let's get to just what this car is. When it was built, Bentley and Rolls-Royce were kissing cousins (I know, eww, that phrase), with both marques sharing production in Crewe on the same platform. That means that, save for its rounded grille, some suspension tuning, and a whole herd of Flying B badges, this model is essentially the same as the contemporary Rolls-Royce Silver Spirit. That means it also shares the Rolls-Royce 6.75-liter OHV V8 engine.

When it debuted in 1993, the Brooklands was meant to be a less expensive (but still very expensive) model slotted under the Turbo R. As such, it was initially available only with a naturally aspirated version of that Rolls engine. That changed in 1996, when the Brooklands got a light-pressure turbo edition, producing 300 horsepower and an impressive 442 pound-feet of torque. That's a good thing, considering this luxury barge is fitted with every comfort and convenience feature the late '90s could offer, bringing the car's weight to over 5,300 pounds. That means reasonable performance and jaw-dropping thirst for premium fuel.

This Brooklands, which the ad claims to be painted in Black Emerald Mica over a parchment Connolly leather interior with spruce trim on the dash and doors, looks to be in fabulous condition. The paint, which appears dark green in the pictures, is accented by elegant but not overwhelming chrome trim and a handsome set of factory alloy wheels.

One notable feature of the Brooklands' cabin is the placement of the four-speed automatic shifter. It sits on the center console, a first for the model line, which traditionally used a column shifter.

The interior, swathed in two-tone leather and elegant wood, cossets passengers like they're in an English drawing room. The only thing missing is the sound of a fire crackling in a hearth. In fact, the ad says nothing is missing from this car, stating categorically that it "needs nothing." In addition to being mechanically and visually sound, the seller notes that the 67,402-mile car comes with a clean title, a passing smog test grade, and a Carfax report offering the kind of dull reading you want on any used car.

Of course, this is a Bentley. And it's a Bentley of a certain age (even older than yesterday's Audi), which means this Brooklands will likely need something in the future. That's to be feared, not eagerly awaited, because parts for these cars are incredibly expensive, and certain maintenance and repair work often requires special tools. Do you possess those? I certainly don't.

That's why anyone interested in a car like this needs to choose the best one they can find and afford. The thing is, these cars are getting very affordable to buy, even in good shape, for a variety of reasons. This one asks $18,000, which I think we can all admit seems like a lot of car for the money. But will it cost far more in the long run? Magic 8-Ball is inconclusive.

What's your take on this Bentley at an $18,000 asking price? Is that a safe bet to slip into the lap of luxury, at least until something major breaks and sullies the experience? Or is even that amount too much to fall into this Brooklands' honey trap?

Los Angeles, California, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#5765. What Risky Car Purchase Ended Up More Reliable Than People Usually Assume?

A long time ago, one of my exes left town for the weekend, and I decided to entertain myself that Saturday with a visit to the nearby motorcycle dealer. I'd been slowly saving up for a bike and just wanted to take a look. Except I didn't just look. They had a bright red 2006 Ducati Monster 620 in the showroom with a price tag on it that read "$2,500." If I'd waited only a few minutes, I would have lost the bike to another customer, but I pulled the trigger just in time and became a Ducati owner.

It wasn't just a Ducati Monster. The '06 models still had the old, round headlight, and the previous owner had put an Arrow carbon fiber dual exhaust on there before selling it. With the meticulous nature with which the cables were all zip-tied, and as clean as it looked, I could tell the previous owner had cared about their bike a lot. They must have loved it, too, because they clearly rode it all the time. The $2,500 Ducati that I bought on a whim became mine with 22,500 miles on the odometer didn't end up as a total disaster.

I rode that Monster all over Long Beach, and then when we moved to Koreatown, I rode it all over Los Angeles, too. I loved that thing so much. Until I got the keys to my Husqvarna, it was the prettiest, most special thing I'd ever owned. The ex didn't love it, but that's what breakups are for. Just kidding, we broke up for other reasons, but I won't pretend my vehicle choices haven't expanded since leaving that relationship. But despite what people usually assume, the red Italian motorcycle that's got a reputation for pricey ownership wasn't an expensive bike to own, and I'd even go as far as to call it dirt cheap.

I can't be the only person who's bought a good, dependable vehicle that other people assume is an expensive, unreliable nightmare, though. I bet plenty of you have owned a few cars that, like my Monster, are reliable in real life, even if normal people assume otherwise. And hopefully, more than a few of you have owned some cars that were somehow, magically the one reliable one that particular company built among a sea of dumpster fires. Whatever it is, head down to the comments to tell us more about the car you bought that ended up being much more reliable than other people expect.

#5762. 2027 Honda Africa Twin Offers More Displacement, Skyhook Suspension, And The Bike's Funniest Trim Level

The Honda Africa Twin is one of the best adventure bikes on the market, but Honda isn't resting on its laurels with its biggest ADV just yet. For EICMA, the company revealed a new generation for the Africa Twin line, bumping the bike from CRF1100L to CRF1150L with tech, styling, and comfort updates to match. The biggest change, though, is a new third sibling in the AT line: Africa Twin and Africa Twin Adventure Sports, meet the Africa Twin Enduro Sports.

The new engine is a 1,131 cc parallel twin, presumably with the same 270-degree crank offset that's so in vogue right now. Honda claims 117 horsepower and 88 pounds-feet of torque from the new mill, though those are global numbers. If they're from the European-spec bike, expect some differences for our U.S. emissions and noise regulations. That engine's bolted to a new frame, one that tucks the fuel tank beneath the seat to lower the center of gravity. It's a trick that worked on my old F800GS, and it'll likely make the new Africa Twin feel smaller than its as-yet-unannounced weight.

The big news out of the Africa Twin line is the new variant, the Africa Twin Enduro Sports. Honda is pitching this as a bigger brother to the CRF450, to which the company says the ES has "front suspension ... specifications" that are "equivalent." It's anyone's guess as to what that actually means on two bikes with different frames, dimensions, and riding styles, but Honda is certainly making it clear that the Enduro Sports is meant to be the most focused off-road member of the Africa Twin family — at least, as focused as any adventure bike can get.

It's always been a bit comical to see people lugging farkled-out GSes through BDRs that would better suit a DR650, but now it seems Honda has made an Africa Twin for people who want to rip through dunes. Is a 500-plus-pound ADV the way to do that? No. Maybe the bike is targeted at Pol Tarres specifically.

While the Enduro Sports is a whole new variant in the lineup, Honda hasn't forgotten the standard AT and the AS. Both get what Honda is very concisely calling "Showa Electronically Equipped Ride Adjustment electronically controlled suspension with Honda Skyhook control," which I will simply be calling "Skyhook" from here on out because, Jesus Christ. Honda claims its Skyhook will adapt damping in near real time to insulate the rider from the texture of the road surface, a touring comfort feature that points toward these two models being more road-oriented than prior Africa Twins — even if the base bike keeps its 21-inch front wheel.

That electronic suspension is paired with the usual bevy of electronic rider aids: Lean-sensitive ABS, traction control, and stability control, all of which can be changed for six different rider modes. Honda of course also offers its dual-clutch transmission, long a staple of the Africa Twin lineup, likely across all three variants.

As usual, the Adventure Sports model remains the most road-touring oriented, with a larger 6.34-fuel tank (Honda didn't say the capacity of the tank on the base and ES models) and a unique fairing design. It retains the 19-inch front wheel of the outgoing model, cross-spoked for tubeless compatibility, and Honda has now given the bike some Gold Wing-tier software: Honda Sensing Ride, a system available on DCT bikes that uses dual front and rear radar units to monitor the area around the bike.

The front radar enables adaptive cruise control, but Honda went one step further and gave its adaptive cruise the ability to come to a complete stop in traffic and resume moving when the car ahead of you does — a system I'm not sure I want on a bike. The radar also enables forward and rear collision warnings, brake assist, and a group ride mode for staggered riding.

The new Africa Twin promises to be a meaningful upgrade on the old model, with more power and a lighter frame, but it seems a more road-oriented bike than the CRF1100L — save of course for the hilariously Dakar-themed Africa Twin Enduro Sports. Sign me up for that variant. I love dumb fun.

#5758. Democrats' Big Win Could Complicate Trump's Emissions Plans

Happy Wednesday! It's November 4, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift — your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition we're looking at last night's election and its fallout on the auto industry, as well as its effects on Elon Musk's companies. We'll also look at U.S. buyers dialing back their automotive luxury spending, and Honda looking at European production.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Midterm elections were last night, and voters overwhelmingly went blue. Not just in battlegrounds like Ohio and Michigan, but in reach states like Texas. Votes are still being tallied, but Mississippi and Alaska may well go blue too. Kansas has its first Democratic senator in nearly a century! Voters have soundly rejected Trump and the Republicans, which could spell some real complications for the party and the automakers that allied with it. From NBC:

President Donald Trump told voters to pretend he was on the ballot in this year's midterm elections.

They did. And they resoundingly rejected both his policies and his Republican Party.

Democrats have captured full control of Congress, NBC News projects, with voters delivering a forceful repudiation of Trump's agenda, coupled with a clear-cut message that Congress has not done enough to provide checks on his administration and needs to do more to address affordability and corruption.

The Trump administration of the last couple years has spent its time rolling back emissions regulations, destroying EV incentives, and generally cordoning off the U.S. automotive market as a little piece of history — somewhere automakers need not innovate to compete. With the legislative branch going blue, though, we may well see new environmental regulations. What will that mean for automakers that cozied up to the MAGA camp? Will we start to match European regulations and resume our EV push? Only time will tell, but all those automakers that returned to V8s may well regret their investments.

Elon Musk was the single largest donor in the 2026 election cycle, having spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates across the country. Not only were his efforts for naught, but his adoptive home state of Texas has gone entirely blue — governor, senate, attorney general, even the railroad commissioner. He's likely to see some complications in his business plans, and the markets are recognizing that. From the Wall Street Journal:

Shares in Elon Musk-led SpaceX and Tesla fell sharply premarket after Democratic candidates swept the midterm elections, handing a defeat to Republicans backed by Musk to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars.

Democratic control of Congress could derail a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, XTB's Kathleen Brooks said.

"While Congress cannot stop a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, they could slow it down via extra scrutiny," Brooks said. "There is now a political risk premium attached to both Tesla and SpaceX that could weigh on their share prices."

Shares have trended upward since market open, but they're still down from yesterday's close. Nathan Johnson, former composer for "Dragon Ball Z" and incoming attorney general of the state of Texas, has already promised to investigate Musk and his companies for corruption. With pressure on both the federal and state levels, 2027 could be a rough year for the world's richest man.

U.S. consumers are getting ever broker, and when you've got less money to spend you're unlikely to go RV or boat shopping. Yet, while automotive toy sales are down, Harley-Davidson is still up. In fact, the company is doing better than it has in years. From the Wall Street Journal:

His purchase helps explain why Harley is bucking a downturn in sales of leisure products: High interest rates, punishing gas prices and broad economic anxiety have dented sales of everything from RVs to boats.

But that downturn hasn't come for Harley. In its primary market of North America, the bike maker has recorded year-over-year retail-sales growth in each of the last four quarters, and is on track for the first full-year increase since 2021. Globally, sales are up 4% so far this year.

The WSJ credits some of this increase to Harley revamping its Tri-Glide line, giving the trikes more power and comfort. Moving those trikes is good for Harley's bottom line, but it's not addressing the fundamental problem of the company: It carved out a market in the '60s, '70s, and '80s, and has largely sold to those same people ever since — buyers too old to keep a million-pound Harley upright. If the company wants new buyers, bikes like its new Sprint are the way it'll get them.

Europe is looking to bring automotive production home to the continent, tariffing car imports to encourage automakers to build in local factories. Plenty of Chinese automakers have already bought in, but one company is still wary to dip its feet into EU production: Honda, which is still just thinking about what it'll do. From Automotive News:

Honda's European chief said the automaker may rebuild a manufacturing presence in the region, depending on the final outcome of new rules in the European Union that will favor locally made cars.

The company has "certainly no intention of leaving Europe," Hans de Jaeger, president of Honda's European unit, said Nov. 4 in an interview at the EICMA motorcycle show in Milan.

Honda registrations across Europe were almost 59,000 in the first nine months of 2026. That's too few to justify building a factory, De Jaeger said, though higher volumes could eventually change the calculation.

It's an unenviable position: Honda doesn't sell enough cars in Europe to justify building new factories there, but it sells enough that it likely doesn't want to leave the bloc entirely. It could share space in a factory owned by another automaker, or eat the tariff costs, but none of those options are perfect. I'm certainly glad I'm not in charge of making that call.

This is how we'll look back on Washington's passage last night of a bill mandating genital inspections for participants in girls' sports. Just, what the hell?

Will we see prices crater after last night's election? Rise based on deadlock within the government, with no veto-proof majorities in the House or Senate? Stay the same?

#5757. SpaceX Starship Will Need To Re-Fuel 22 Times In Space To Make It To The Moon

As NASA plans to send astronauts back to the surface of the Moon in 2028, there's still the small matter of figuring out how to get them there. While the Artemis II mission proved that we can send people around the Moon and bring them safely home, the space agency needs a way to take astronauts out of the Orion capsule and down to the actual ground. The original plan was for a SpaceX Starship to fulfill this duty, and that could still be the case. But delays in the development of that ambitious rocket caused NASA to re-open the contract, which allowed Blue Origin to toss its hat in the ring. Still, SpaceX insists it will fend off this challenge from a rival billionaire-owned space company and win the contract all over again. The only thing standing in its way: the minor fact that it has to refuel the Starship in-orbit, something never done before and that SpaceX hasn't even attempted yet. Oh, and it has to do it many, many times. How many? Great question.

The NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel recently announced that, by their calculations, a Starship would require fully 22 in-orbit refuelings to get that one single rocket to the Moon's surface, per Ars Technica. Again, the total number of times that any rocket has ever done this is zero. Specifically, the plan from SpaceX is to launch one Starship into orbit to act as a fuel depot; then launch many other Starships to load up that first one with fuel; then launch a final Starship to take on that fuel from the depot and head out to the Moon.

If 22 sounds like an insane number to you, you're not alone: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on the social media platform X, which SpaceX owns, "Actual number will be more like 6 to 8." That makes for quite a broad range of estimates. The reason this is so fuzzy is because the fuel we're talking about here isn't gasoline, but rather a mixture of liquid oxygen and methane. This actually boils off in the vacuum of space, so how much fuel can be transferred depends on the efficiency of the technology involved. Technology that has never actually been tested in orbit.

Currently, SpaceX plans to perform its first test of orbital refueling in early 2027, just a little over a year before it will theoretically do it for the Moon landing. If that doesn't work, well, SpaceX's lunar ambitions are in trouble. Even if it does go well, and there are absolutely no issues whatsoever with this unprecedented capability, there's still the small matter of actually launching all of these rockets. Right now, the still-in-development Starship only launches once every few months. Musk claims it will be launching weekly by early 2027, just months away. And then he further claims it will launch twice a week by the end of 2027. Let's just say that would be, ah, truly remarkable if it happened.

For once, let us be optimistic, and believe in words. If these words be true, and Starship truly is launching twice-weekly, then launching 22 refueling Starships (plus launching the initial "depot" Starship) would take... three months. And that is assuming no failures, either of the rockets or of the fuel transfer process. That's reduced to three weeks if you also believe Musk's figure of six launches. At least Musk has never once lied about his companies capabilities! If for some reason you don't believe in that launch cadence, then total refueling will take potentially years. Either way, that would amount to the most complicated endeavor NASA, or any space entity, has ever attempted.

By contrast, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin has a much simpler plan to get to the Moon. It's still complicated, let's be clear, but less so than SpaceX. The company's proposal calls for a mere four launches of its New Glenn rocket, assuming it doesn't explode and destroy its entire launchpad, again. The first three would park a booster stage in orbit; the fourth would put a Blue Moon lunar lander into orbit, where it will collect all the booster stages, stack them together, and then blast off towards the Moon. That is a wild dance all its own, but it doesn't require figuring out how to transfer any fuel.

If you're wondering where the actual astronauts are, don't you worry: they're on a completely different rocket altogether. The Space Launch System (SLS) rocket carries the Orion capsule into orbit with all the astronauts on board. The capsule then continues on from Earth orbit to lunar orbit on its own, as the Artemis II mission demonstrated. Somewhere along that path — whether in high-Earth orbit, high-lunar orbit, or low-lunar orbit (this part still isn't nailed down) — the Orion capsule will have to dock with either the Starship or the Blue Moon, depending on who wins the contract. The lander will then land, the astronauts will enjoy a nice walk around another world, and then the lander will return to lunar orbit. Then it's back aboard the Orion capsule and then back to Earth.

Sounds easy! Basically, a lot has to go right for NASA to make that 2028 landing date. How it shakes out in practice depends on how well a lot of untested equipment and procedures work. Then again, if you were to go back to the 1960s, the Apollo program wasn't exactly any more precedented, or safer. In that decade, though, NASA did have a lot more testing demonstrations before going for the Moon. This time around, the agency wants to get there faster.

#5756. 1976 Pontiac Trans Am For Sale With 7 Miles After Restoration Pairs 4-Speed Stick And 455 V8

For those looking to channel your inner Burt Reynolds from "Smokey and the Bandit," WeBe Autos (via Hemmings) has this lovely black-and-gold Trans Am for sale that's nearly the perfect match. Except, it's a 1976, not a 1978, so it doesn't feature the quad-headlight front-end that the movie car had. If that's what you want, however, this 1978 example or this 1979 one that's done roughly 22,000 miles should be of interest. Neither of them, mind you, is in black, nor do they feature a 455-cubic-inch V8 or offer the three-pedal experience like the '76 example we have here.

Unlike the movie car, though, this Trans Am is a hardtop coupé. But it has undergone extensive restoration and has only done seven miles since. And yes, it has the Screaming Chicken hood decal, or the "Rising Phoenix" if you're part of that camp. So what's the asking price for this 1970s muscle-car goodness? That'd be $72,495. Although it may not be as sophisticated as the latest BMW iX3 (also a $70,000 ballpark proposition), the 455 V8 and four-speed combo has enough personality and aura to challenge whatever these modern-day "computers on wheels" can offer.

Character assessment aside, what you get for your money is a well-finished exterior, a beautifully detailed engine compartment, an exceptionally clean underbody, and a beautifully restored all-black interior. While the Endura-style bumpers and Honeycomb wheels stand out as exterior highlights, the classic Trans Am instrumentation, custom Autosound audio system, and factory-style dashboard come across as some of the notable attractions on the inside. Sure, it might not be a T-top nor feature the movie car's front fascia, but then again, Bandit's companion was actually a 1976 Trans Am with a '77 front end.

Classic Industries and Hemmings reckon there were four cars used in total, while Autoweek counts five, but the important thing is that all Trans Ams used in the movie started out as '76 Special Edition 50th Anniversary cars with the updated '77 front end. Pontiac had to get creative because the movie's production began before 1977 models were actually available. And the engines you saw (or rather heard) on screen weren't part of the 1977 lineup at all. While Classic Industries reported the stunt cars retaining the 455 V8, in reality, you could not have optioned the motor in a 1977 car — it was retired after the 1976 model year.

Setting aside this bit of "Smokey and the Bandit" trivia, you can probably already tell how the Trans Am listing we have ties in with all this. It's a 1976 car in the right paint scheme, with the 455 and a four-speed manual thrown in for good measure. More importantly, there's no deception here, and it looks nothing like a 50-year-old hunk of metal.

Is the near-$73,000 asking price too much? That depends on whom you ask. It's a lot of money for something that old. Despite the restoration, that 455 was part of the Malaise Era lineup, which famously neutered a lot of high-performance V8s. Given that the listing mentions "emissions equipment present," it's unlikely that things are any different here. Still, for someone who likes '70s Americana, is an ardent fan of movies, or, above all, a true-blue Pontiac enthusiast, this Trans Am should hold plenty of appeal. Assuming, of course, they have the means to afford it.

#5755. “War” Secretary Pete Hegseth Endorses 15 Minute City Model

You just can’t make this stuff up. While conservatives around the world are waging holy war against the “15 Minute City” concept, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has gone all-in on the idea. His newly announced “Fortress America” military resilience plan includes a new vision for military bases that embraces walkability and quality of life. If that sounds like the 15 Minute City plan in action, it is. Oh, lordy…

Walkable communities are as old as the hills. That’s what people did before automobiles hit the scene and cities were organized around cars. Credit for applying the walkability model to 21st century urban planning goes to the Franco-Colombian scientist Carlos Moreno, who formalized the 15 Minute City concept in 2016. The idea got a further boost of attention when the Mayor of Paris, Anne Hidalgo, pitched walkable, bike-able neighborhoods as part of her successful re-election campaign in 2020.

The COVID-19 lockdown of 2020 was also a pivotal moment, with a surge in work-from-home households drawing attention to the need for local resources as a matter of survival and resiliency in case of a widespread emergency.

The 15 Minute City model covers a lot of ground, but the basic idea is that people should be able to do their shopping, recreation, socializing, and other essential routines within walking or biking distance from their homes, making cars largely optional within the neighborhood. Walkable access to schools and health care is also part of the plan.

The argument for 15-minute cities (also called 15-minute neighborhoods or 15-minute communities) is also pretty straightforward. Walking is healthier than sitting in a car. Avoiding injury or death from car accidents is another plus. Walking also reduces carbon emissions, and it saves money on gas.

In addition, walkability levels the playing field, so to speak. Everyone in the 15-minute zone has walkable access to basic resources, regardless of whether or not they can afford a car. In other words, there is a significant equity and inclusion element to the concept…

…and, that’s where the trouble kicks in. In 2022 the World Economic Forum posted an article by Lisa Chamberlain, the founder of the urban communications and business firm Strategies for City Builders. Chamberlain describes a 15 Minute City as characterized by diversified, mixed-use neighborhoods built to withstand shocks like COVID-19 and climate change.

“As climate change and global conflict cause shocks and stresses at faster intervals and increasing severity, the 15-minute city will become even more critical,” Chamberlain emphasized, with a further emphasis on equity and inclusion:

“Specifically, communities that foster and maintain social and economic relationships don’t have to be wealthy, but they do need to be walkable and safe, with both residential and commercial buildings intact. And, I would add, for 15-Minute Cities to thrive, not just survive crises—and this cannot be stressed enough—they must also have plenty of mixed-income and equitable housing, as well as digital access.”

It didn’t take long for the conspiracy machine to kick into action around the globe. In February of 2023, for example, the Australian news organization ABC radio summed up the 15 Minute City conspiracy theory thusly:

“To some, it’s an urban planning concept that promotes sustainable and healthy living.

“To a small group of others, it’s a plot by ‘tyrannical bureaucrats’ to take our cars and control our lives, which could lead to a real-life Hunger Games scenario.”

“Limiting cars and promoting pedestrian or bike access is framed as a slippery slope to government-run, open-air prisons,” ABC continued.

Yikes! ABC also cites the Canadian psychologist Jordan Peterson. who railed against “idiot tyrannical bureaucrats” who “decide by fiat where you’re ‘allowed’ to drive…and, make no mistake, it’s part of a well-documented plan” (emphasis added).

Ohfergawdsakes, of course there is a well documented plan, and it’s called urban planning. And, that’s where the US Department of Defense comes in.

On September, in a move that sailed under the CleanTechnica radar, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the new “FORTRESS America” plan, with FORTRESS representing “Federal Operations for Resilience, Troop Resources, Energy, Supply, and Survivability.”

Stripping away Secretary Hegseth’s testosterone-fueled purple prose in the September 30 announcement, FORTRESS AMERICA applies the 15 Minute City urban planning model to major Defense Department bases in the US, ensuring they can operate independently of civilian infrastructure for a sustained period of time. That includes everything needed to support community life in addition to the supplies needed to sustain military operations.

FORTRESS America even goes beyond the initial 15 Minute City concept. As envisioned under the “Next Great American Base” element of the program, a central feature of the plan consists of access to a reliable source of on-site energy.

Don’t just take my word for it. “The program aligns basing and infrastructure projects to ensure they are collectively advancing toward greater independence,” Hegseth stated in the official order, with independence referring to the capability to sustain operations within a facility that is cut off from civilian resources. In other words, sustainable urban planning for military facilities.

Hegseth tasked the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment to carry out the new order. The base design part of the order was passed along to Dale Marks, the Assistant Secretary for Energy, Installations, and Environment.

Marks did not let the 15 Minute City grass grow under his feet. In a public presentation on October 29, he emphasized the importance of building quality of life into a sustainable model for military facilities in the US.

“Let us build installations worthy of the warriors who call them home,” Marks emphasized. “The nation shouldn’t expect warfighters to focus on high stakes, multidomain operations when they come home to base housing with black mold, failing plumbing and leaky roofs.”

“Substandard living conditions are not minor inconveniences. They are an active drain on morale, combat readiness and our retention of top-tier talent,” Marks elaborated.

It’s not just a matter of rehabbing military housing. In the presentation, Marks made the case for a full blown 15 Minute City model. “The Next Great American Base will include a compact, walkable concept with premier schools, advanced healthcare and town centers that foster community,” Marks continued, neatly summing up the fundamentals of 15 Minute Cities in a nutshell.

Marks anticipates that state governors and other stakeholders will compete to see where the first “Next Great American Base” will be constructed. Once complete, the new facility, and its 15 Minute City, will serve as a model for future projects.

As for the on-site power generation angle, nuclear energy gets the pole position — for now. As Marks and Hegseth both emphasize, though, speed is of the essence. Results are demanded within months, if not weeks. That leaves plenty of room for solar-enabled microgrids to throw their hat into the FORTRESS America ring. After all, if speed-to-power is the name, solar and batteries are the game…

Image: The 15 Minute City model calls for walkable, bike-able access to basic services and resources, a concept that has been embraced by none other than the US Department of Defense (courtesy of Rutgers University).

#5753. FDA Panel Largely Pans Trial Data for Myopia Eye Drops

— Atropine slowed progression but clinical meaningfulness, robustness of data questioned

The regulatory status of a low-dose atropine eye drop formulation for myopia remained unresolved following a day-long FDA advisory committee meeting, but closing comments did not bode well for SYD-101.

The Dermatologic and Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee (DODAC) did not vote to recommend for or against approval of the eye drops, but panelists' responses to key questions posed by the FDA suggested the evidence from a phase III trial of SYD-101 did not meet standards for approval.

"Basically, the summary is that, although the clinical trial is positive, it's not a robust outcome that would meet the standard presented to us as the reason for approval by the FDA," said DODAC Acting Chair Michael X. Repka, MD, of the Johns Hopkins Wilmer Eye Institute in Baltimore. "The issue of missing data remains sort of difficult for this committee to manage."

Primary support for the approval application came from the SYD-101-001 randomized trial (also known as the STAR trial) comparing two doses of atropine sulfate ophthalmic solution versus vehicle to slow myopia progression in 852 pediatric patients 3 years or older. The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with myopia progression exceeding 0.75 diopters at 36 months.

The primary analysis showed that 39.5% of patients randomized to the 0.01% solution met the primary endpoint as compared with 49.3% of patients randomized to the control group (P=0.0452). The 0.03% treatment arm did not achieve statistical significance versus the control group.

The difference between the 0.01% arm and vehicle translated into progression slowing of 0.079 diopters per year or a cumulative difference of 0.21 diopters versus control. In a briefing document prepared for the meeting, FDA staff said the difference, though statistically significant, was not clinically meaningful and that the magnitude of benefit decreased over time.

Additionally, primary endpoint data were missing for 26% of patients in the 0.01% treatment arm and 23% of the control group. Sensitivity analyses showed the outcome data were influenced by different assumptions about the statistical impact of missing data.

The staff report also noted that the trial failed to show a significant reduction in axial length, which raised questions about the treatment's potential to alter myopia-related structural changes. Half of the participating centers did not measure axial length, and measurement was not uniform at the centers that did. Additionally, "external evidence from other randomized controlled trials conducted in non-Asian Western populations has generally been unsupportive of the efficacy of 0.01% atropine."

Summarizing the panel's comments regarding the clinical meaningfulness of the differences observed in the trial, Repka said, "The [committee] basically considered the clinical meaningfulness of the observed efficacy profile uncertain, both because of the magnitude, the question of just a shift or delay in myopia progression by the 6-month or 1-year cycle, and also the lack of corroboration on axial length in those centers that were able to perform it. [The committee] would recommend to manufacturers in the future to consider including axial length as a primary or key outcome measure."

The panel also appeared to agree with FDA staff that the published literature did not provide confirmatory evidence, beyond the SYD-101-001 trial, that would rise to the standards necessary for approval.

"When I look at the other studies, they were not as well performed or designed as the [SYD-101-001] study we're discussing," said panelist Timothy G. Murray, MD, of the University of Miami Bascom Palmer Eye Institute. "The size, stratification, and randomization that was done was a plus. The way that the data was looked at is a plus. The other studies fall far below that standard, and therefore, I wouldn't consider that substantial evidence or a standard for approval."

In a separate report for DODAC, representatives of Sydnexis noted that the SYD-101-001 trial was designed with input from the FDA. They emphasized that the trial met the prespecified primary endpoint and that the levels of statistical significance increased in a multiple-adjusted analysis (P=0.0226). Data for the key secondary endpoint also achieved statistical significance for the 0.01% solution versus vehicle (P=0.0002).

Though acknowledging missing data, Sydnexis stated that "missing efficacy data and discontinuations were not meaningfully imbalanced across groups. All prespecified missing-data sensitivity estimates favored SYD-101 0.01%, with treatment estimates generally consistent with the primary result."

DODAC panelists did not dispute the statistical significance of the primary endpoint but rather questioned the robustness and clinical meaningfulness of the results. Murray said the lack of robustness "calls into question our ability to interpret the data further."

Alex Kaizer, PhD, a biostatistician at the University of Colorado Anschutz in Aurora, noted that confidence intervals for efficacy data approached 0%, making the results susceptible to small changes.

"I think what this means to me, with the discussion around the potential clinical significance and the heterogeneity of the patient population, is that it feels like more data is truly needed to understand, especially in younger ages and fast progressors, what the benefit would be," he said.

Acknowledging that the treatment seems promising and is approved elsewhere in the world, Kaizer added, "These borderline results do make it challenging, because if just a few people change their outcome, it could change the result suddenly to a very different discussion than the one we're having today."

Throughout the meeting, several speakers noted that dozens of studies have demonstrated atropine eye drops' efficacy in myopia and that low-dose formulations are available in many nations, but not the U.S. Clinicians in the U.S. can and do prescribe low-dose atropine eye drops, but the medication is available only through compounding pharmacies.

The DODAC meeting had its genesis in a complete response letter the FDA sent to Sydnexis in October 2025.

"The FDA acknowledged in the complete response letter that this primary endpoint was met but stated its view that the data do not support the effectiveness of low-dose atropine in children with myopia," company officials stated in a press release. "No deficiencies were noted related to safety or product quality."

In response, Sydnexis submitted a formal dispute resolution request to the FDA, which subsequently scheduled the DODAC meeting to consider the evidence in separate presentations by FDA staff and speakers representing Sydnexis, including several pediatric ophthalmologists.

The next step is up to the FDA, and no timetable for a decision was announced at the conclusion of the DODAC meeting.

#5752. Nabrawind’s Crane-Free Wind Towers Face a Supplier Test

Spain’s Nabrawind has developed a way to install exceptionally tall wind turbine towers without bringing an enormous crawler crane to the site. Its Nabralift system uses a tubular upper tower supported by a three-legged steel structure. Hydraulic equipment raises the assembled turbine while modular sections are inserted below it near ground level. The lifting frame can then be removed and used on another installation. This addresses genuine logistical and construction problems, particularly at remote sites where specialist cranes are expensive to transport and where wind can interrupt conventional lifting operations.

The company has progressed beyond demonstration-scale hardware. In September 2026, UL Solutions issued type certification for Envision’s 7.8 MW turbine on Nabrawind’s 188-meter tower. Fortescue is using 17 of those tower configurations at the 133 MW Nullagine wind project in Western Australia’s Pilbara region, where construction is underway. Nabrawind previously erected a 160-meter prototype in Spain in under two weeks and has supplied smaller commercial towers in Morocco and France.

The engineering benefits are credible. Nabrawind reports using roughly 20% less tower steel than comparable conventional tubular designs and reducing foundation concrete by as much as 80%, depending on the design and site. Those are supplier claims rather than independently established savings across all wind farms. The potential to avoid large cranes, simplify transport and raise turbines in windier conditions could also matter substantially to total installed cost and construction schedules. High hub heights only earn their keep when those costs are justified by the electricity generated over the project’s life.

The current deployment has an unusual commercial structure. Fortescue acquired Nabrawind in September 2025 and is building Nullagine to serve its own mining operations. Fortescue has the capital, internal electricity demand and industrial incentive to support a technology it owns. Successful installation in that context would be important evidence of construction performance, but it would not establish that an unrelated wind developer can finance and maintain the same system under ordinary third-party commercial arrangements.

Nabralift’s proprietary construction approach creates a procurement issue. Conventional tubular towers can be sourced from several qualified manufacturers, and experienced contractors can compete for much of their construction work. A developer selecting Nabralift currently depends on one supplier for the core tower system, specialist lifting knowledge and associated support. Wind turbine original-equipment manufacturers also create supplier dependencies, but concentrating another critical part of the project in a proprietary installation system requires its own contract and risk assessment.

A type certificate provides valuable technical assurance about the certified turbine-and-tower configuration. A lender or insurer still needs enforceable delivery schedules, long-term warranties, repair and maintenance provisions, clarity on replacement parts, and a workable remedy if the supplier’s capacity or commercial priorities change. These questions become more important when a wind farm must operate for 25 years or longer and there is no qualified alternative provider of the same system.

Nabrawind’s next important proof point is an independently developed and financed large wind farm that accepts those risks on commercial terms. Qualified installation partners, credible long-term service arrangements and greater competitive capacity could make its engineering advantages easier for developers to buy. The 188-meter tower has earned technical attention; its broader market depends on financing and procurement confidence catching up with the machinery.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Nabrawind’s self-erecting design, Fortescue’s Nullagine deployment and the supplier concentration that independent wind developers would have to manage. It follows my earlier assessment of 300-meter wind towers, where construction economics were the central challenge.

#5751. Scandal-Ridden Cadillac F1 Owner Putting Team Up For Sale After Just One Year

The long-awaited entry of an American factory team was viewed as a coup for Formula 1. Billionaire financier Mark Walter is now looking to sell the Cadillac F1 Team after a single F1 season. While the team has failed to score a point in its maiden campaign so far, the sale would help him dodge scrutiny amid federal investigations into alleged self-dealing. Walter's TWG Group is in negotiations to sell a significant team stake at a $3 billion valuation.

Walter amassed a sports empire over the past 15 years. His investment firm Guggenheim Partners purchased the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2012 for $2.15 billion. Walter personally owns 27% of the MLB franchise. Since the acquisition, the Dodgers have alarmingly amassed over $1 billion in deferred payroll obligations on their way to three World Series titles. TWG would expand into racing in 2024, purchasing Andretti Global and its F1 entry bid. The company spent over $1 billion on the Cadillac F1 Team before its debut race in Australia earlier this year, nearly half that total was an anti-dilution fee.

How could Walter afford to do all of this? According to The Wall Street Journal, the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating how TWG-owned insurance companies lent billions of dollars to Walter's other enterprises. IndyCar fans are familiar with these insurance companies, seeing Delaware Life and Gainbridge logos plastered on Andretti's cars. An internal review found that $20 billion in loans weren't disclosed to financial regulators. Walter presumably needs to repay said $20 billion as soon as possible.

The TWG firesale began in August. Walter sold the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion to Josh Kushner's Thrive Capital. The deal was negotiated over a weekend. He added the NBA team to his sports empire just last year for $10 billion. After the Lakers deal, TWG denied that the Cadillac F1 Team was for sale. Despite the denial, Fenway Sports Group is the favorite among several bidders to buy the F1 team. The company currently owns the Boston Red Sox, Liverpool F.C. and RFK Racing in the NASCAR Cup Series.

The Cadillac F1 Team's sudden sale could be viewed as an opportunity for another automaker to enter Grand Prix racing, but General Motors also owns a stake in the team. With that constraint, FSG is the most logical choice to keep the team on its current course as GM develops its in-house F1 power unit program. Even without the federal investigations, Cadillac has had a rough start. The team has yet to score its first point. Team principal Graeme Lowdon was replaced in August. American F1 hopeful Colton Herta has yet to secure a Super License, partly due to the team misreporting Herta's past results to the FIA after believing an error on the IndyCar website.
