#5750. Last Night's Blue-Tomic Bomb Probably Blasted Away Musk's Tesla-SpaceX Merger Dreams

Voters delivered a stunning rebuke of Republicans and everything they stand for Tuesday night, taking control of both the House and the Senate in a wave of wins that just kept coming. Democrats kept winning, again and again, wave after wave. A bluekkake, if you will. And while that's great news for the stock market, the Middle East, healthcare, trans kids' safety, and so many other hugely important issues, voters also rejected Elon Musk and his billionaire meddling. We won't be able to get rid of him overnight, but at least Musk's dreams of a Tesla-SpaceX-Twitter-xAI merger are probably dead.

If you remember, Musk has long been reported to want his companies all under one roof to complete Tesla's tranformation into an AI/robotics company (or stop making cars without crashing the stock price). xAI already merged with Twitter and stuck Musk's antisemitism-spewing, CSAM-generating chatbot in Teslas, then merged with Spacex ahead of its IPO. As previously reported, Musk had then ordered Tesla to look at spinning off its China business to help his main division merge with SpaceX more easily. Musk also floated the possibility with investors, and one of the Trump administration's lasting legacies will be its love of corporate mergers, so it sounded plausible.

With Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, likely finishing with 258 Representatives and 55 (or 56!) Senators, the left doesn't just have power, it has a mandate from the voters to put a stop to everything the Trump administration is doing. Raskin will chair the House Judiciary Committee, Garcia will chair the House Oversight Committee, and both have promised investigations into any criminal activity that's taken place. That's not exactly fertile ground for a major corporate merger, especially after Musk attempted to inflame a race riot in Ireland, campaigned for Germany's Nazi-adjacent AfD party, and blew hundreds of millions of dollars trying to elect Republicans.

Yes, our friends over at the Tesla Takedown kept a running thread going last night, highlighting every race Musk lost and how much money he wasted. Nearly two dozen races, all won by Dems, even though a Republican billionaire tried to buy their elections. Per Vanity Fair, Musk dumped an eye-watering $474 million into this election, and he still got kicked in the nards. He could have given $50,000 to 9,400 people and still wasted less of his money.

Democrats who haven't been bought off by the crypto and AI lobbies have been sounding the alarm in recent months about the dangers of any one person having as much power as Elon does. The man has the power to slow down Ukraine's military's internet, and the prospect of combining SpaceXAI with the most valuable car company in the world makes a lot of regulators nervous. Expect it to be a fight with the centrists in the party, but Dems are more likely to try to weaken Musk's power, not hand him a win.

Because our election system is weird, Republicans won't lose power until January and could theoretically rush the merger through. But even the Motley Fool — a website that published "Prediction: SpaceX Stock Will Go Parabolic After Nov. 6" the day both Tesla and SpaceX shares plunged — doesn't think that's likely. In an article foolishly calling the merger "inevitable," the MFers timeline is still "within the next 12 months" not "before January." They also admit many factors, including antitrust enforcement could be a problem for the merger.

With Dems winning a huge mandate to govern, Republican politicians should be less willing to stick their necks out for that eternally sticky loser, too, so calling it "inevitable" is certainly a take. More importantly, Republicans have a much more important activity on their agenda than facilitating this merger. With Trump humiliated and unable to run for a third term anyway, Republicans are leaderless. When they move from depression to anger, they're going to start pointing fingers. Infighting and power struggles are inevitable unless Republicans just give up completely.

With Tucker Carlson and Marjorie Taylor-Greene-whatever waiting in the wings, the far-right giving up isn't likely either. So expect Republicans to be distracted, Democrats to feel emboldened, Jeffries and Schumer to remain spineless cowards, and Elon Musk to struggle getting any attempt at a Tesla-SpaceX merger off the ground. That's probably something Elon's sad about, but for the rest of us, it can only be good news any time Elon's dreams go up in smoke.

#5749. Upfront TAVR May Be the Way Forward in Moderate Aortic Stenosis, Trial Suggests

— First randomized study to evaluate TAVR versus clinical surveillance in moderate AS

Upfront transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was more protective against death and heart failure events compared with clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis (AS) with at least one at-risk feature, the randomized PROGRESS trial showed.

At 2 years, a composite endpoint of death from any cause or a heart failure event occurred in 16.7% of patients in the upfront TAVR group versus 23.9% of those in the clinical surveillance group (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93, P=0.02 for superiority), reported Philippe Généreux, MD, of the Gagnon Cardiovascular Institute at Morristown Medical Center in New Jersey, during the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference, hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

In addition, TAVR with the balloon-expandable Sapien 3 platform had a safety event rate of 5.9% at 30 days, which was well under the prespecified 13.7% performance goal, and the bulk of events were hospitalizations for device- or procedure-related complications (5.6%).

The study was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"Moderate AS is not benign, and these patients would benefit from earlier referral to a valve clinic for comprehensive evaluation to establish the optimal management strategy," Généreux concluded. "Rather than waiting for progression to severe AS, PROGRESS supports TAVR for patients with moderate AS and at-risk features."

Importantly, the trial has follow-up planned for 10 years. In the meantime, Généreux said that the PROGRESS trial has already identified the "optimal time" for intervention in AS considering the balance of safety and efficacy.

Among the clinical surveillance patients who started out with moderate AS, 57.4% eventually underwent a delayed aortic valve replacement (AVR) by 24 months. Of these patients, over 80% had progressed to severe AS.

Meanwhile, the TAVR arm showed the "best hemodynamics that we ever saw" with the Sapien valve, Généreux reported, citing the effective orifice areas, mean gradients, and minimal paravalvular leaks achieved. "The future will tell, but I strongly believe based on the data today ... [that] this is the optimal timing of intervention to ensure optimal treatment for a patient given that we can treat a second time."

"This disease progressed faster than [we] expected," he stressed. "You need to follow these patients. You cannot abandon them."

During a press conference, panelist Pinak Shah, MD, of Mass General Brigham in Boston, called the trial a "truly practice-changing study" that "really underscores the importance of close follow-up and the fact that AS is not a benign disease."

The results also suggest a drastic widening of the pool of TAVR candidates.

A large registry study, also by Généreux and colleagues, recently showed that patients with moderate AS outnumber those with severe AS by nearly 2:1, and over a quarter of those with moderate AS in this study progressed to severe AS by 2 years.

Ultimately, Généreux argued for doing away with the dichotomy of moderate versus severe AS altogether and moving towards intervention on "clinically significant" AS instead.

For their trial, the investigators sought participants who were at least 65 years old with moderate AS plus at least one at-risk feature. The majority were recruited from the U.S. (87.1%), with a minority coming from sites in Japan, Australia, the Netherlands, Canada, and Switzerland.

Out of 1,294 patients screened, 744 were randomized 1:1 to transfemoral TAVR or once-yearly clinical surveillance from October 2021 to January 2024. Mean age was 78 years, and 39% were women. The Society of Thoracic Surgery risk score was about 3.0%, and fewer than half of patients were deemed low risk per the heart team. New York Heart Association class III/IV symptoms were observed in about 35% at baseline. The Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) score was about 64 on average.

The top at-risk features that qualified people for the study were valve-related symptoms (96.4%) and diastolic dysfunction (43.8%).

Généreux reported that 91% of enrolled patients had moderate AS in terms of both moderate aortic valve area (AVA) criteria and peak velocity/mean gradients. The mean AVA was 1.2 cm2, the mean gradient was just over 25 mm Hg, and the peak velocity was 3.3 m/s. About one in four people had an elevated aortic valve calcium score.

The effectiveness endpoint was a composite of death (8.4% vs 7.3%, HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.67-1.93) and heart failure events (10.8% vs 19.0%, HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.37-0.81). Of note, a heart failure event had to meet all three criteria: new or worsening heart failure symptoms, two or more objective indications of new or worsening heart failure (physical, laboratory, imaging, and/or invasive findings), and escalation of heart failure treatment.

Altogether, the number needed to treat for benefit at 2 years was 14 in the trial.

Separately, as a standalone endpoint, heart failure hospitalizations were fewer in the TAVR arm (7.4% vs 14.9%, HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.30-0.77). However, the composite of death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization did not statistically give TAVR an edge (17.7% vs 23.3%, P=0.07).

As for health status improvement, the mean KCCQ score was 79.6 points in the TAVR arm at 30 days. The proportion of patients alive with an improvement of 10+ points in KCCQ score at 1 and 2 years favored TAVR (39.0% vs 23.2%, P<0.001).

Généreux noted that when it came to delayed AVR in the control arm of the study, KCCQ scores generally dipped before the delayed procedure, followed by a substantial improvement 30 days later.

The incidence rate of new permanent pacemakers was 13.0% with upfront TAVR versus 10.4% with clinical surveillance.

Of note, limiting wider generalizability, PROGRESS had notable exclusion criteria that barred people with unsuitable anatomy for transfemoral TAVR, significant clinical comorbidities, very low ejection fractions, or prior aortic valve replacement or valvuloplasty, among others.

"Certainly, we have to be very careful with patient selection," commented Shah. "For most, the lifetime management is going to be important ... A lot of these patients are probably going to come back for repeat procedures."

#5748. How MRD is powering the next wave of precision oncology

How MRD is powering the next wave of precision oncology" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Cancer care is shifting beyond the detection of visible disease. A new generation of molecular residual disease, or MRD, testing can detect tiny traces of ctDNA that may remain during or after treatment, offering an additional way to identify disease when traditional approaches may not yet reveal it. Dr. Rick Baehner, Divisional Vice President, Chief Medical Officer, Precision Oncology, Abbott cancer diagnostics, explores why MRD represents the next chapter of precision oncology and how the next-generation Oncodetect® test could help move cancer care from reactive treatment toward more proactive monitoring.In this video interview with Kelly Hogan of Fierce Healthcare, Baehner explains how MRD testing can provide molecular insights into some of oncology's most pressing questions: Is treatment working? Is cancer truly gone? Has disease returned? He also explores why sensitivity is critical, particularly when tumor burden is low, including in low-shedding cancers and as ctDNA levels fall during and after treatment. Baehner explores the science behind whole-genome sequencing-based MRD tests and looks ahead to what broader adoption could mean for oncology workflows, clinical decision-making and patient outcomes. As MRD testing becomes more integrated into everyday care, he argues that cancer monitoring may become as individualized as cancer treatment itself. Watch the interview to learn why the next era of oncology may be defined not only by how we treat cancer, but by how quickly and intelligently we anticipate its return.

#5746. BMW Just Went 186 MPH In The New Alpina 7 Series

Thanks to spy shots, we already knew BMW was hard at work cooking up the next Alpina B7 and that it'll have a V8 that sounds pretty great. The brand has now come out with official footage of the car doing high-speed testing at the Nardò test track, exceeding 186 mph. What, did you think the special label version of BMW's flagship sedan would be slow? For reference, the last-gen Alpina B7 already had a top speed of 205 mph, so 186 was frankly table stakes. That said, the speed itself arguably isn't what BMW is flexing her — it's the peace with which that speed is achieved.

"Speed has always been baked into the Alpina brand's DNA," said BMW Alpina vice president Oliver Viellechner. "However, we are not just interested in top speed alone. What matters is how natural, stable and confident it feels to drive at that speed." Internally, the brand apparently calls these cars "distance-shrinking" machines; autobahn weapons made to cover literal continents in great speed, style, and serenity.

You might recognize the name Nardò, by the way, from "Nardo Gray," that primer-like paint color popularized by Audi. The Nardò Ring, a 7.8-mile test track in southern Italy owned by Porsche and shaped like a perfect circle, is where that comes from.

Other confirmed details now include Alpina-signature 20-spoke lightweight wheels (peeping at the sidewall shows a diameter of 22 inches) wearing specially made tires that feature an extra layer of foam inside allowing for peak high-speed stability and comfort. Four oval exhaust tips emit a "rich, deep sound," and BMW says max torque out of that V8 is available "across virtually the entire rev range," while engine management software and throttle mapping is tweaked for smoothness over aggression. Gearbox tuning, too, has been revised to accommodate the bump in horsepower and engine speeds.

This new B7 (or whatever BMW will choose to call the next Alpina-ized 7 Series) will be the first production car made under the joint BMW Alpina brand. BMW announced that it had acquired Alpina back in 2022, but didn't take full control over the tuner until the beginning of this year. The new BMW Alpina 7 Series will be unveiled next year.

#5745. Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin

Midstream Health nabs $20M series A to help hospitals recover lost margin" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Health systems are losing margins they’ve already earned, according to Sumit Kadakia, CEO and co-founder of Midstream Health. The startup bets that artificial intelligence can improve hospital margins by finding money that is already embedded in contracts and transactions.

Midstream Health, an autonomous financial operations platform for health systems, picked up $20 million in series A funding to expand its AI financial platform. The company is expanding across a customer network representing more than $100 billion in annual operating expenses and over 250 hospitals nationwide.

Valtruis led the financing round with continued participation from Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Foundry and CommonSpirit Ventures, bringing Midstream’s total funding to $29.2 million. Fairview Health Services and Keck Medicine of USC are among the newest health systems to join the platform, alongside CommonSpirit Health, Mount Sinai Health System and Houston Methodist.

Midstream says its AI financial platform helps health systems find and recover margin across revenue and cost, strengthening the financial capacity needed to keep investing in care and serving their communities.

"We bring all of a health system’s data together, across pharmacy, supply chain, managed care, revenue and cost, into a single source of truth, and then put AI agents on top of it to find and recover money the system is owed. We call it the 'second financial brain' for a health system," Kadakia said in an interview.

He added, "That’s a lot of technical talk for a pretty shocking problem: hospitals are multibillion-dollar enterprises, and most of them don’t have any form of managerial finance."

With that data foundation in place, Midstream Health's domain-trained agents proactively flag and prioritize cost-saving and margin opportunities such as missed rebates, pricing errors, payer underpayments and policy-driven denials.

Kadakia describes the platform as "an army of agents that runs alongside a health system’s finance and supply chain teams, never sleeps, and is constantly finding and recovering margin."

The company plans to use the fresh funding to expand its product and engineering capabilities, particularly as it moves into new verticals. It also plans to continue formalizing its sales and marketing functions and building a dedicated research function that owns its underlying data connections, Kadakia said.

Health systems are facing a financial sustainability crisis, fighting to protect razor-thin margins. More than 110 rural hospitals have closed over the past 20 years, and another 720—representing roughly a third of all rural hospitals—are at risk of closure. Much of what’s slipping away is money health systems have already earned, buried in their own contracts and spend.

According to Kadakia, one system can have thousands of contracts across supply chain, pharmacy and managed care, each with its own pricing tiers, rebate triggers and amendments. "Nobody has time to check every one against what the system actually buys and pays, so a six-figure rebate can disappear because one form was missed. Meanwhile, most healthcare AI money has gone into the claims fight between hospitals and insurers. Every dollar one side wins, the other side loses, and the total cost of care goes up. Deflationary AI will make care cheaper to deliver, and the most direct way to do that is making sure [that] health systems collect what their contracts already say they’re owed. Margin that stays buried in a contract never reaches patients," he said.

Kadakia says he has a personal perspective on the issue—his father practiced at two rural West Virginia hospitals that have since closed.

"In today's challenging healthcare environment, we have to be thoughtful about how we manage our resources and continually look for opportunities to operate more efficiently," said James Hereford, CEO of Fairview Health Services, in a statement. "By leveraging AI-driven financial operations, we can improve financial performance, allowing us to focus more resources on delivering care to our patients and communities."

CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest nonprofit health systems in the U.S., was an initial investor in Midstream and became one of the first healthcare partners chosen to implement and validate the platform through integration with supply chain operations. After implementation, Midstream's AI agents provided "measurable gains within days, surfacing opportunities like missed rebates and underpayments," according to Daniel Barchi, CommonSpirit Health's chief information officer.

"It is a closed-loop AI system that transforms financial intelligence into real-time action, delivering a data foundation, visibility and execution capability," Barchi said in a statement.

Across its customer base, Midstream claims it has identified more than 1,500 financial recovery opportunities this year, from six-figure rebates buried by a single missed form to systemic payer underpayments. Early Midstream partners are projecting more than 5x ROI this year. The platform is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026, the company claims.

In the near term, Midstream is on pace to reach $100 million in client savings by the end of 2026.

"The longer-term piece is what I’m most excited about, because I think this enables a renaissance in value-based care. Value-based care was built on an unstable foundation. To take on risk, a hospital needs a clear view of what care is actually costing it and why, and the systems to give hospitals that view were never built. If we give them that foundation, they can take on more risk, and that’s how you start to deflate the arms race between payers and providers," Kadakia said.

In the current financial environment, health systems need solutions that can improve their financial position quickly, noted Mike Spadafore, managing director of Valtruis. "We’re backing Midstream because it’s built first-of-its-kind infrastructure to turn complex financial data into action. Where enterprise healthcare technology can take years to demonstrate value, Midstream delivers within the quarter," he said.

AI is intensifying an ongoing financial battle between health systems and insurers, and data shows that this AI "arms race" is driving up short-term healthcare costs. The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association estimates hospitals’ AI coding tools added nearly $1 billion in costs over two years, and insurers are answering with AI of their own.

"Patients, employers and taxpayers pay for that arms race. The next decade should be judged by a simpler test: does the technology bring total cost down? That’s the standard we hold ourselves to," Kadakia said.

#5744. Bay Area Air District Moves Forward with Nation’s Strongest Water Heater Standards

Health advocates, environmental groups, heat pump installers, local electeds celebrate decision as.

SAN FRANCISCO — The Bay Area Air District voted today to move forward with the strongest clean appliance standards in the nation, putting millions of Bay Area homes on a path to switch from gas water heaters to zero-emission alternatives. Beginning in 2028, households will be required to install water heater appliances that meet clean air standards as old gas units burn out, with exemptions approved today for low-income households and complicated installations.

Gas appliances in Bay Area homes and buildings generate more smog-forming nitrogen oxide pollution than all of the region’s passenger cars combined. The Air District estimates its clean appliance standards for water heaters and furnaces could prevent up to 85 premature deaths and 15,000 asthma attacks each year.

The switch also saves families money. New research from RMI finds $360 in annual savings for Bay Area residents from switching from gas water heater to a heat pump. Analysis from SPUR projects $315 million in rebates for home energy efficiency will be available in the next three years to support the transition.

The vote follows thousands of public comments in support of the standards, despite an industry-backed opposition campaign linked to oil interests.

Supporters of the standards released the following statements:

“The research makes it clear that climate policies and affordability go hand-in-hand and today the Bay Area is taking the historic step of making clean home appliances the standard for a better future,” said Melissa Yu, Campaign Strategist for Clean Heat, Sierra Club. “A transition toward zero-emission gas heaters will reduce a key source of smog pollution, launch programs to help get more people access better technological solutions and lower energy costs. Today’s vote is a victory for cleaner air and for energy affordability.”

“Today’s vote will supercharge the job growth we’re already seeing at heat pump businesses like mine, opening new pathways for early-career Bay Area workers looking for family-sustaining wages and meaningful work. The Bay Area Air District showed real leadership in approving these standards. We’re proud to be on the front lines of equipping homes with energy-efficient technologies that cut energy bills, clean the air, and make homes more comfortable,” said Owen Krebs Grimsich, CEO and owner of 1-888 Heat Pumps.

“Today, the Bay Area chose clean air over fossil fuel pollution. Under these standards, when a household’s gas water heater wears out, it will be replaced with cleaner, more efficient technology like a heat pump, so millions of residents will breathe easier and save money on their energy bills. The Bay Area Air District showed real leadership, and the rest of the country should follow its lead,” said Tony Sirna, Deputy Policy Director for Buildings at Evergreen Action.

“Today’s vote is a big win for clean air, lower utility bills, and climate leadership,” said Berkeley City Council member Igor Tregub. “The Bay Area is moving forward with the nation’s strongest water heater standards, and millions of families here will breathe cleaner air as a result. These standards build in the flexibility we need to make the transition workable, while growing the market for clean technologies that lower bills and create good jobs.”

“Today, the Bay Area Air District said yes to saving lives and no to gas industry attempts to slow progress to clean our air,” said Fernando Gaytan, senior attorney on Earthjustice’s Right To Zero campaign. “The Bay Area is now one step closer to making non-polluting appliances the  norm thanks to the leadership of board members and staff. This policy will show the rest of the country what’s possible.”

“Today’s vote is a step forward for cleaner air, healthier homes, and a more affordable energy future. By advancing these standards, the Air District shows we can move away from polluting gas appliances without leaving families behind,” said Sam Fishman, sustainability and resilience policy manager, SPUR. “Bay Area cities, utilities, and regional programs are taking the important steps to invest more than $120 million annually in home electrification and energy-efficiency incentives. With these tools, we can make our homes safer for our planet and our health, too.”

“As regional leaders in building electrification, Acterra sees this vote as a vital win for local communities and public health,” said Lauren Weston, Executive Director at Acterra: Action for a Healthy Planet. “Transitioning to zero-emission heat pump water heaters clears toxic nitrogen oxide pollution from our neighborhoods while lowering utility bills and accelerating equitable access to clean, energy-efficient technology for all Bay Area households.”

“The Air District Board’s vote today to support the implementation of Rule 9-6 is a watershed victory for healthy and safe communities, moving from our dependence on fossil fuels to a cleaner, greener source of energy,” said Leslie Alden, Executive Director of Act Now Bay Area. “The Air District staff, the experts, the working groups, and so many dedicated members representing the Bay Area worked tirelessly from 2023 show once again that the Bay Area leads the way.”

General Motors is recalling 67,380 Chevrolet Blazer EVs And Cadillac Lyriqs, Vistiqs, and even Celestiqs because under specific circumstances, a software defect can cause a temporary loss of braking ability. According to the NHTSA recall report, GM is aware of 20 minor accidents due to the fault, two of which resulted in minor injuries. Fortunately, the condition only arises at low speeds, but any loss of braking is a deeply concerning and dangerous occurrence. Two-wheel-drive Cadillac Lyriqs are not included in the recall, and the only Blazer EV trims involved are SS and Police Pursuit Vehicles.

Cadillac Lyriqs are hit hardest by the recall, which includes 474 2023 Lyriqs, 22,819 2024 Lyriqs, 11,926 2025 Lyriqs, 9,322 2026 Lyriqs, and 44 2027 Lyriqs. The recall also includes 13,627 2026 Vistiqs and 5,175 2027 Vistiqs, as well as 51 2025 Celestiqs, and 31 2026 Celestiqs. (This is one of our best glimpses yet into how many Celestiqs have been sold.) The only Chevrolets included in the recall are 562 2024 Blazer EVs, 2012 2025 Blazer EVs, 1,314 2026 Blazer EVs, and 23 2027 Blazer EVs. VINs are already searchable on NHTSA's website, and the remedy comes in the form of an over-the-air update for owners who have opted in to those, otherwise owners will have to take their vehicles to dealerships to have the software update downloaded.

The conditions that lead to the temporary loss of brake function are very specific. According to the recall report and GM's testing, "when the brakes are lightly applied at low speeds during a sharp turn and the vehicle encounters a bump or depression – such as at the end of a driveway – a momentary release and reapplication of the brakes may cause the software's slip calculation to misinterpret wheel movement. In some instances, this may result in a temporary loss of braking. The phenomenon is unique to certain vehicles equipped with performance all-wheel drive (pAWD, RPO X0E) and is resolved when the brakes are applied again."

GM already recalled 21,469 all-wheel-drive Lyriqs for a similar issue in 2024, but it found that vehicles built with the software changes following that recall and vehicles that already received the software update from that recall are still susceptible to the conditions described in the new recall, and they need the latest update. The latest software update corrects the slip calculation in the vehicle's brake system control module that causes the temporary loss of braking, which coincidentally is the same claim made on the 2024 recall. Hopefully this time it actually fixes the problem.

If you drive one of the cars included in the recall, be aware of the possibility of braking loss, and remember that if you experience braking loss, normal brake function should return on the next brake press. Dealers should already be notified of the recall, but owner notification is estimated to begin on December 14.

#5741. Who Controls the Battery in Your Driveway?

Tesla brought home power backup to America. In Australia, an update is switching it off. North American owners just got Powershare with Powerwall. Australian owners of existing Teslas got a software update that appears to block the third-party gear they use to power their homes. It is a test case for who really controls the battery in your driveway.

Mark Purcell is an electrical engineer and energy advocate based in Noosa Heads, Queensland, Australia. He owns two Teslas and a bidirectional DC charger, and has been a member of the Australian Electric Vehicle Association since 2022. He has contributed content to CleanTechnica previously.

On 12 October, my Model Y ran my house. Through a Sigenergy bidirectional DC charger in my garage on Australia’s Sunshine Coast, it supplied about 25 kW to my home. The battery in my driveway holds several times the energy of a typical home battery, and I have already paid for it.

That may not last. Owners in several countries report that Tesla software from the 2026.38 branch, rolling out since October, cuts third-party discharge within minutes. On the Tesla Motors Club forum, owners describe power stopping after about three minutes with a battery management alert, or after 15 to 20 minutes whatever the load. The old Camp Mode and Service Mode workarounds no longer help. Drive Tesla Canada has covered the reports. EleJoy, Tlyard and Sigenergy users are all affected, and Tlyard now warns customers that Tesla’s 2026 software detects “simulated charging” and may cut the power link.

The release notes? “Security improvements” and minor fixes. Nothing about switching off a function owners use every day.

Here is the part that should interest readers everywhere. The same 2026.38 branch delivered Powershare with Powerwall home backup to owners in the US and Canada. That is a good thing. Tesla has finally joined Ford, GM, and Kia in letting the car back up the house.

Australia did not get it. Tesla Australia has said Powershare cannot be retrofitted to existing vehicles, and here Powershare is vehicle-to-load only. So, for every existing Tesla on Australian roads, third-party equipment is the only way to put the car to work for the home. If the software now blocks that equipment, Australian owners are left with nothing: not Tesla’s solution, and not anyone else’s.

The Tesla Australia owner’s manual says: “Do not use the Battery as a stationary power source. Doing so voids the warranty.” Tesla’s own Australian warranty page is narrower. It excludes damage caused by third-party adaptors or chargers, not the whole warranty.

Australian law is narrower again. Under the Australian Consumer Law, statutory consumer guarantees cannot be signed away by a line in a manual. Apple found this out when the Federal Court ordered A$9 million in penalties over the “Error 53” affair, after Apple told customers that third-party repairs had cost them their rights. American readers will recognise the shape of this argument from the right-to-repair fight.

Australia is a world leader in rooftop solar and is now subsidising home batteries at scale. The next step is obvious: the biggest battery most households will ever own is already parked outside. Bidirectional charging is how that capacity reaches the home and, in time, the grid.

That whole idea depends on interoperability. If one carmaker can switch off discharge overnight, through an over-the-air update the owner cannot roll back, and without saying so, then every bidirectional charger is a bet on that carmaker’s goodwill. Chargers bought in good faith become stranded. Competing suppliers lose access to the fleet. Grid operators lose flexibility they are counting on.

The ACCC, Australia’s competition and consumer regulator, has already named “denying interoperability” as conduct that can distort competition in digital platform markets. A car that decides which charger it will talk to is a platform in all but name.

I am deferring Tesla updates on both my cars, so I am also missing whatever genuine fixes they contain. I have asked Tesla in writing to hold updates until it confirms discharge will keep working. I have lodged a complaint with the ACCC under Australia’s competition and consumer laws. I have also asked the Australian Electric Vehicle Association, the national voice of EV users, to back it.

Tesla may have a real safety or engineering reason. If so, it should say what it is, and show why a less restrictive answer would not work: certified partner equipment, discharge limits, or a published interface that charger makers can build to.

Three things, and they apply well beyond Australia. Carmakers should disclose functional changes in plain language before they ship. Owners should be free to use the bidirectional charger of their choice. And regulators should set interoperability rules for vehicle discharge, as many already do for solar inverters. If we can make inverters speak a common language, we can stop cars locking out the chargers they plug into.

My car still powers my house. It does so only because I have stopped it updating. No owner, in any country, should have to choose between a current car and a working home battery.

“I am looking forward to the discussions around this topic,” David Waterworth, who helped get this article published, adds.

#5740. Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude

Athenahealth launches tool to bring patient health records into Anthropic's Claude" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Electronic health record company athenahealth is opening up patient health records to outside AI assistants, starting with Anthropic’s Claude, through a new connection designed to give patients personalized answers based on their clinical data.

The new server solution, athenaPatient MCP, uses the Model Context Protocol to connect Claude directly with the athenaOne platform. Patients authenticate using their athenahealth patient portal credentials and decide what information Claude can access, according to the EHR company. Credentials are not shared with Claude.

Paul Brient, athenahealth's chief product and operations officer, said that information is encrypted in transit, patients control what information is shared, and they can revoke access at any time. "Once the connection is established and patients approve what types of data they would like to share, the rest is between Claude and the patient," he told Fierce Healthcare in an interview.

Brient noted that AI can meaningfully reduce complexity and help patients play a more active role in their care. "At its core, this is about helping patients get value from their own healthcare data," he noted.

Athenahealth is committed to responsible AI integration, company executives said.

Patients are turning to generative AI, like Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT, to interpret lab results, medication instructions and other medical information. More than a third of U.S. adults (34%) have used AI assistants for health-related purposes, including looking up symptoms to understanding a diagnosis, according to an August Pew Research Center survey. This trend reflects a growing expectation for immediate, conversational health guidance, but also introduces new governance challenges, athenahealth executives noted.

"Claude is the first connection we’ve enabled for athenaPatient MCP, but it's not intended to be the only one," Brient said. "Anthropic has been a strong launch collaborator because of its approach to responsible AI development. But our strategy isn't built around a specific AI model. The AI landscape is moving incredibly quickly, with new models and tools coming to market seemingly every week. We designed athenaPatient MCP with that reality in mind and built it on a Model Context Protocol (MCP) that has become an industry norm for AI interoperability."

Claude Pro and Max users in the U.S. can add the athenaPatient MCP connector within their Claude settings. Patients can then ask Claude questions about their health information using natural language. With a patient’s permission, Claude can reference information such as lab results, medications, vitals, health conditions, diagnostic reports, immunizations, visit history, allergies, procedures and care plans to generate personalized answers based on their clinical data, instead of generic or incomplete information, athenahealth executives said.

"Patients often have questions about their health records between visits, from what a lab result means to what to ask at their next appointment," Syed Mohiuddin, head of healthcare at Anthropic, said in a statement. "athenahealth is giving patients a way to bring their own records into Claude when they choose to, so they can explore those questions and feel more confident and prepared in conversations with their care team."

Athenahealth's EHR is a cloud-based, open platform, Brient noted, and the company's objective is to "create a secure way for patients to use their health information with the AI assistants they choose," he said.

The company plans to expand access to other models, but Brient did not provide any details about additional integrations.

The company built athenaPatient MCP to connect to general-purpose AI assistants rather than build those generative AI capabilities entirely within athenaPatient.

"It's not our job to decide which AI assistant patients should use. Patients are increasingly using AI tools in their daily lives, and I expect that trend to continue. If we've learned anything over the last few years, it's that people will gravitate toward the experiences that work best for them. Healthcare shouldn't be isolated from that reality," Brient said.

"At its core, this is about giving patients access to their health information in the places where they want them—safely, of course. Our patient-facing connector is consistent with our broader interoperability capabilities. Consumers increasingly expect their personal data to integrate into the digital tools they use. Healthcare shouldn't be an exception," he said.

Some providers have raised concerns that as patients increasingly use AI chatbots to interpret health records and lab results, it will drive an uptick in follow-up messages to physicians. Brient noted that giving patients an easier way to connect their health records to AI tools helps patients better understand the information their providers have given them and have more informed questions.

"One of the realities of healthcare is that patients often leave an appointment with more information than they can reasonably absorb in the moment. Lab results often arrive after the patient has seen their doctor. Questions come up after the visit. Medication instructions get forgotten. That's not a criticism of patients or clinicians. It's just reality," he said.

"When patients have a stronger understanding of their healthcare situation, conversations with their care teams tend to be more productive. From the clinician perspective, we were equally focused on what this should not do. We did not want to create additional work for clinicians. A recurring theme across our product strategy is reducing work while improving outcomes. The best healthcare technology helps patients become more engaged without creating more administrative burden for clinicians," Brient noted.

Athenahealth provides EHR software, revenue cycle management and patient engagement solutions to small and independent provider practices. A year ago, the company unveiled new AI features for ambulatory providers as part of a larger upgrade to an "AI-native" athenaOne platform. This summer, the company rolled out more than 80 new AI features for RCM operations on its AI-native athenaOne platform.

Athenahealth executives describe the launch of athenaPatient MCP and the connection to Claude as just the first step, suggesting a broader strategy of allowing patients to use AI tools with their health records.

"The immediate focus is helping patients securely access and understand their health information through the AI assistants they choose to use. Looking further ahead, I think it's reasonable to expect both the number of AI assistants and the capabilities available through them to expand. One of the reasons we're excited about MCP is that it creates a standardized way to provide context to AI systems. Context is what makes AI particularly useful. Without context, AI can provide general information. With context, it can provide a more detailed, personalized set of information and is less likely to lead you astray," Brient said.

Major EHR companies are moving forward with AI integrations to connect patient data with AI tools OpenAI's ChatGPT for Healthcare now integrates with Epic's EHR to enable authorized clinicians to access and summarize patient information from medical records within ChatGPT or directly in supported Epic workflows. That integration can now pull together clinical notes, lab results, medications and specialist documentation, the company said in a blog post.

Oracle’s AI-powered patient portal allows patients to chat directly with their electronic health record using a conversational interface built on OpenAI frontier models.

In healthcare, MCP creates a common framework for connecting AI agents to clinical systems and data.

"I think it's still early, but this is an important trend to watch," Brient said. "One of the challenges with AI is that intelligence without context isn't particularly useful. In healthcare, context must be accurate, permissioned, secure, and current. That's a much harder problem than simply connecting a chat to a data source."

What makes MCP interesting, he noted, is that it provides a framework for connecting AI systems with the context they need while preserving appropriate controls and governance.

"Whether MCP ultimately becomes the interoperability layer for AI in healthcare remains to be seen, but I think the demand for this type of interoperability is only going to increase. Patients and providers are already using AI. The question is whether healthcare data can participate in those experiences safely and effectively," he said, adding, "I feel good about where the industry is headed, and I believe standards like MCP can play an important role in getting us there. But we're still in the early innings, and much work remains. Our goal is straightforward: reduce friction, maintain trust, and help patients and providers benefit from advances in AI without compromising security or control."

#5739. Tesla Allegedly Misled Thousands Of South Korean Customers About 'Full Self-Driving'

Usually, when we tell you that Tesla has gotten into hot water for misleading folks about its "Full Self-Driving" Level 2 driver assistance system, it has to do with Tesla overstating just how capable of a system it is. That's not the case in South Korea, though, where the Texas-based automaker has allegedly vastly overstated the legality of FSD usage and charged customers for it nonetheless. Now, tens of thousands of Korean Tesla owners are looking for answers.

Tesla apparently markets FSD in South Korea despite the fact that it knows the majority of its cars can't legally use the program in the country, the complaint from an advocacy group alleges. That means it can't be activated on the car. Soon, the complaint will be filed with the Korean Fair Trade Commission, a consumer protection agency, according to Reuters. Tesla will have to answer for why it marketed FSD to prospective buyers for years, even collecting the $6,726 lump-sum payment required for activation, even though it couldn't legally be used.

Currently, just 20% of Teslas registered in South Korea can legally use FSD because they're built in the U.S., according to a preliminary testimony given by Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk last month. Those specific cars meet U.S. vehicle-safety standards that South Korea recognizes as part of a free trade agreement. The thing is, most Teslas on the road in South Korea are manufactured in China, where no such agreement exists. It was only recently that Tesla started the process of obtaining FSD certification on China-made vehicles, even though it has been charging customers for the software for over three years.

Right now, it's not totally clear how many customers in South Korea bought FSD subscriptions on ineligible vehicles, but the automaker has sold over 170,000 China-made vehicles in the country since 2023, Reuters reports. The company continued to market FSD as sales of ineligible China-manufactured vehicles surged in South Korea in recent years, and last year, 99% of new Teslas sold in the country couldn't legally use FSD.

The complaint alleges that last year, Tesla promoted FSD as "coming soon" and posted a demonstration video filmed in South Korea without clearly disclosing that the tech could only be used in a tiny fraction of the vehicles it was selling, according to Reuters. The consumer advocacy group accused Tesla Korea of deceptive marketing and has asked the KFTC to issue a temporary cease-and-desist order on marketing FSD for ineligible vehicles, impose fines and refer the case to state investigators.

It may be an uphill battle, though. Just last month, a court in Seoul dismissed a lawsuit filed by Tesla owners seeking refunds for the FSD option, Reuters reports. The court rejected the claim that Tesla had failed to deliver the driver-assistance system. Instead, it put the onus of the issue on regulatory and legal restrictions that had limited the company's ability to roll out future functions.

#5738. Darolutamide Improves Metastasis-Free Survival in Very High-Risk Prostate Cancer

— Phase III DASL-HiCaP trial showed a 58% reduction in the risk of metastasis or death

Adding darolutamide (Nubeqa) to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and radiation therapy significantly improved metastasis-free survival in patients with very high-risk prostate cancer, according to findings from the phase III DASL-HiCaP trial presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress. At 4 years, the metastasis-free survival rate was 95% with darolutamide versus 88% with placebo.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, investigator Tamim Niazi, MDCM, of McGill University in Montreal, discusses the findings, including which patients may benefit most from treatment intensification, the safety results, and why he considers the data practice-changing.

Following is a transcript of his remarks:

So DASL-HiCaP, it was a phase III randomized trial assessing the role of the additional darolutamide to 24 months of androgen deprivation therapy plus a locoregional radiation therapy for patients who are at DASL very high risk, so specifically selected patients who are very high risk based on DASL criteria. We'll talk about this in a minute or two.

But what this study actually showed for these patients who are at a very high risk of recurrence and relapse is that adding darolutamide increased the metastasis-free survival by conventional imaging. It's important, it's not by PSMA [prostate-specific membrane antigen], it's by conventional imaging at 4 years, from 88% in the placebo arm to 95% in the darolutamide arm, with a hazard ratio of 0.48. That is a 58% risk reduction in favor of darolutamide.

So how we define very high risk in DASL-HiCaP is not the usual high risk and not the same thing as STAMPEDE very high risk.

For patients who had prostate in place for primary radiation therapy, the very high risk was defined as either grade group 5, Gleason 9-10, or pelvic lymph node disease. Any of those would've made participants eligible. And for participants who had a grade group 4, meaning Gleason 8, they had to have an additional risk factor, either a clinical T2b or higher, a PSA [prostate-specific antigen] more than 20, or radiological T3a or higher.

On the other hand, for patients who had salvage radiation therapy after radical prostatectomy, those patients had to have their PSA either persistent after surgery, meaning having not gone to zero or rising within 12 months to a 0.1 or higher. They would've been eligible to participate as long as they met the eligibility criteria, either a grade group 5 with a Gleason 9 or 10 of course, or pathological or clinical pelvic lymph node positive. Similar to primary radiation therapy, patients in salvage were also eligible if they had grade group 4, and were also eligible if they had an additional risk of pathological T3a or higher.

But to us, it is a more higher-risk patient population compared to other studies, for example, ENZARAD, but not STAMPEDE.

Both groups received the contemporary doses of radiation therapy and hormonal therapy, higher doses of 78 Gy and higher in primary setting, 64 Gy and higher in salvage setting. And of course the pelvic radiation therapy was mandated in the study.

So the standard treatment was given very well to the contemporary stage, and then it was for darolutamide to show an improvement. So it did. It decreased the risk of metastasis by 58%. To me, I think it is practice-changing and it definitely defines a new path for patients who are at a very high risk of recurrence.

Not only did it significantly improve metastasis-free survival, the adverse events were pretty similar between the two groups. Specifically, there was no additional cardiovascular toxicity by adding darolutamide. It was almost identical between the two groups. And furthermore, the addition of darolutamide to locoregional radiation therapy did not cause new emergent toxicity when it comes into a combination of treatment in this investigation.

#5737. Elon Musk Threw Away $474 Million (Or More) … But May Benefit From Failing

Some people think Elon Musk has lost his mind. Others think he’s always been a charlatan and has just had an insane amount of luck. Some people think he’s a genius and that everything he touches will turn to gold. And then there’s also a decent portion of folks who think he’s an absolute idiot about some things but brilliant — or at least very clever — when it comes to others. Whatever you think of Elon Musk, though, there’s no denying he just threw away about half a billion dollars.

Musk reportedly spent at least $474 million on the midterm elections (because one individual is allowed to do that, apparently), and yet his picks — the key people he supported — got completely crushed. The politicians he spent all of that money to get elected did not get elected, and were actually not even close to getting elected. Apparently, voters in their jurisdictions thought they were horrible choices, sometimes historically so. Imagine if all of that money he spent had been spent on something good and useful instead! (Perhaps saving the lives of starving, poverty-stricken children and babies around the world? Perhaps stopping the spread of horrible diseases, since the US government has dropped such efforts on several threats? Perhaps to provide subsidies for electric vehicles, like Tesla sells, since Republicans in Congress and Donald Trump killed those? Perhaps to use solar power instead of fossil fuels to power AI data centers?)

Why did Elon Musk spend a whopping half a billion dollars (or more) on the 2026 midterm elections?

I know there are some people who don’t see this, but it’s been clear for a while that the following things are true about Elon Musk:

Musk largely targeted Texas with his political spending, and Texas had an epic, historic blue wave. Something that has been dreamt about for decades came true in dramatic fashion despite Elon Musk spending hundreds of millions of dollars to try to stop it. Ironically, Democratic politicians are the ones who support electric vehicles and solar power, key segments of Musk’s empire. It was California, led by Democrats, that birthed Tesla Motors and enabled it to grow and develop into an industrial behemoth. It was US policies under Democratic presidents and Congresses that also provided critical help for years upon years. So, despite Elon Musk’s worst instincts and biggest efforts politically, will his businesses actually do better under the newly elected Democratic leadership? Perhaps there are some corporate issues that need reigned in or need better regulation, and perhaps people Musk brazenly and often quite rudely campaigned against will squeeze down extra hard on his corporate actions, but policymakers who support cleantech over fossil fuels should, overall, mean more good news than bad news for Tesla and its broader mission, right?

Sure, Musk threw away $474 million and lost bigly, but is he going to be better off from failing in his efforts to pick the people running his current home state and representing it in the US government? What are the actual risks he and his companies face from the people he heavily campaigned against winning their elections? What are the benefits he and Tesla will get from fossil-loving, pollution-peddling Republican politicians no longer running the show in Texas and in Congress? One has to wonder.

By the way, one of the key people Musk campaigned against, James Talarico, has a message specifically for him. “Texas is not for sale,” Talarico said. Musk spent at least $150 million to try to get Talarico’s opponent elected. “The people of Texas delivered a crystal-clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale,” Talarico added. “The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people, and we’ve got to make sure it stays that way.” What do the people want? Well, the people want clean air, clean and cheap energy, and less money in politics. Shouldn’t all of those things help Musk? On that last one, after all, if he wasn’t allowed to pour so much money into politics, he wouldn’t have thrown away half a billion dollars.

#5736. NASA's Swift Space Telescope Re-Enters Atmosphere With Five Times More Risk Of Casualties Than Anticipated

On Wednesday, NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a space telescope that's been in orbit since 2004, finally re-entered Earth's atmosphere above Indonesia. However, it appears to have done so with a risk of casualties five times beyond what NASA technical standards mandate. How and why this happened isn't immediately clear; NASA Public Affairs Specialist Alise Fisher told Jalopnik, "In the leadup to Swift's Nov. 20, 2004, launch, NASA determined the risk was consistent with mission requirements as allowed by agency policy." Somewhere between launch and reentry, that risk assessment shifted. It's unlikely that anybody made a specific mistake; this is probably the result of, well, space being hard. Still, it does highlight that our main defense against the detritus of astronomical ambitions is pure luck.

Swift is only crashing to Earth because it ran out of fuel to stay in orbit or adjust its trajectory. To NASA's credit, it did throw $30 million at a private company in an unprecedented attempt to rescue Swift with another satellite that would pull it back up into safe orbit. Sadly, the rescue satellite itself failed, dooming Swift to this fate.

In formal terms, Swift suffered an "uncontrolled reentry," which basically means it had no propulsion and just fell from space. NASA's own requirements, most recently updated in 2021 but going all the way back to 2001, state: "For uncontrolled reentry, the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall be less than 0.0001 (1:10,000)." If you're not aware, there's no actual law requiring that satellites de-orbit in some sort of safe way that won't, you know, crash into a city or kill anyone. So our shield against the skies is just statistics. This is the threshold at which NASA feels the risk is acceptable. For reference, in all of history, just about 10,000 satellites have de-orbited, so... statistically we're due. And that was before we were putting tens of thousands of satellites up every few years.

In Swift's instance, however, NASA played its cards a little close to its chest. For one thing, it did not put out a risk assessment for the reentry, which is unusual. Then, in the middle of a longer announcement, the agency mentioned that Swift's risk of human casualties was actually "1 in 2,100." That's a risk of human injury or death five times beyond what it was meant to be.

Fortunately, the odds appear to have resolved in our favor. There are no reports of anyone being struck by space debris from Swift. Most of the satellite was expected to burn up during reentry; the trouble would come from whatever survived, likely dense pieces like the telescope lens or the reaction wheels. If any of those made it to the surface, there doesn't appear to have been a person around it.

That's a roll of the dice, though. At some point, as thousands of satellites de-orbit per year in our new megaconstellation era, laws should be passed to manage this formally. That would likely mean requiring controlled reentries, when the satellite still has a little fuel left to navigate to a safe spot out in the ocean. The other option, which companies like SpaceX have been pursuing, is to design the satellite to burn up entirely on reentry. The issue there is what effect all that vaporized metal might have on the atmosphere. Scientists don't yet know the answer, for the simple reason that there was never a reason to ask that question before. Now, the health of our planet may depend on it.

As space gets busier and busier, more and more will fall to us down here from up there. Up until now, the power of statistics has kept us safe. But eventually, a 1 in 10,000 chance is going to happen. Especially if some of those chances turn out to be riskier than intended.

#5735. Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike

Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 date for open-ended strike" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital are set to strike in the coming weeks after failed contract negotiations, in what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

Brigham and Women's Hospital said in a statement it received notice from the Massachusetts Nurses Association (MNA) on Nov. 1 about an open-ended strike beginning Thursday, Nov. 12 at 7 a.m.

"While we had hoped to avoid another strike, we are prepared to continue providing safe, high-quality care throughout any work stoppage, building on our experience and extensive contingency planning," the statement read. "We deeply value and respect our Brigham nurses and remain committed to reaching a fair and responsible agreement. Our latest offer provides market-leading compensation and competitive benefits while recognizing our responsibility to our patients, our entire workforce and the long-term financial sustainability of Brigham and Women’s Hospital."

Negotiations with MNA are set to resume Nov. 9, the hospital said.

MNA said in a statement negotiations will focus on "securing a fair contract that meets the needs of the nurses, their patients and the community members they serve." Nurses are seeking the following terms as part of a fair contract, per the union:

"We are ready to strike but are equally prepared to negotiate a fair contract that protects patient care, respects nurses, and averts the strike," said Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital. “Brigham nurses are resolved to fight for as long as it takes for patient safety and the professional respect we deserve.”

Union nurses at Brigham and Women's Hospital voted to reject management's "last, best and final offer" on updated contracts, potentially steering the dispute back toward what could be the largest open-ended nurse strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association had previously scheduled the strike for Oct. 14, but postponed to give its members a chance to vote on the proposal from Mass General Brigham, the hospital's parent system. The union said it has requested to resume contract negotiations this week, with the hospital responding in its own public statement this it "is prepared to maintain uninterrupted care and respond to any steps the union may take."

MGB's rejected offer would have retained the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The union has said it is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

“This vote shows the resolve of Brigham nurses, who are fighting for patient safety and for the professional respect we deserve," Kelly Morgan, chair of the union's bargaining committee for the hospital, said in a weekend release. "It’s [time for] MGB to return to the table ready to negotiate in good faith to reach a fair agreement that recognizes the value of Brigham nurses and the expertise they offer for the care of some of the region’s most complex patients every day.”

Brigham and Women's Hospital said it was "disappointed" by the rejection, and that its proposal "reflected the hospital’s commitment to investing in our nurses while supporting long-term sustainability, including meaningful compensation and benefit enhancements that kept Brigham nursing pay among the highest in the market."

Notably, the announcement of the member vote's outcome coincided with news that MGB has begun a new round of layoffs affecting both clinical and operational programs. The unspecified number of cuts reflect a financial need to further adjust operating MGB's structure even after roughly 1,500 people were laid off in 2024, the system said.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have lifted their notice of an Oct. 14 strike after their union and Mass General Brigham management made progress toward a potential contract deal late Saturday night, the sides said in statements.

The 4,000-member open-ended strike would be the largest in state history if launched, and follows months of contract negotiations between the health system and the Massachusetts Nurses Association (see that coverage below).

A formal deal has yet to be struck, though the union said it agreed to call off its 10-day strike notice "given the complexity of the agreement and the impact of a potential strike on our nurses and the community." The proposal is being presented to members for a vote, which might yield a new 10-day notice if rejected.

Brigham and Women's Hospital, in a Sunday statement, said its "last, best and final offer ... reflects significant movement on several of the union's priorities while maintaining a responsible approach to supporting nurses, patients and the long-term strength of the hospital."

It added that the offer retains the hospital's existing nursing wage progression system of annual 5% step increases until 20 years tenure, with the addition of two additional 2.5% increases at the top of the prior structure. The withdrawn notice also saved the hospital from having to implement its contingency staffing plan of hiring temporary nurses.

"We are thankful the MNA has pulled its indefinite strike notice and will allow its members to vote on the hospital's final offer," the hospital said. The union's statement did not specify the timing of that vote.

Editor's note: On Oct. 2, the Massachusetts Nurses Association announced an Oct. 14, 7:00 a.m. start time for their strike if no deal is reached.

Nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have voted to authorize an open-ended, 4,000-member strike that could become the largest nurses’ strike in Massachusetts history.

The Massachusetts Nurses Association announced the 93% in favor vote that was held Thursday evening. No date has been set yet by the union, which is legally required to give employer Mass General Brigham (MGB) 10 days' notice.

“Brigham nurses have made clear that we are prepared to stay on strike for as long as it takes to win a contract that protects our patients and respects the nurses who care for them,” Kelly Morgan, a labor and delivery nurse and chair of the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MNA Bargaining Committee, said in the union’s announcement. “An open-ended strike is a serious step that will undoubtedly create a healthcare crisis in Massachusetts. MGB can prevent the strike by returning to the table and negotiating the contract our nurses need to keep providing world-class care.”

Contract negotiations between the sides have been ongoing since last November, with the prior agreement expiring on March 31. In July, the nurses (plus an additional 450 home care clinicians) conducted a one-day awareness strike that was also a record breaker for the state and the first at Brigham and Women’s, a flagship hospital and founding member of the nonprofit system.

Demonstrations have continued in the weeks since, including a rally held earlier this week outside of an MGB-hosted World Medical Innovation Forum, where bargaining members painted a contrast between executives’ conversations with investors on AI and the demands of their clinical workforce.

The hospital, in statements given to press, said “we remain committed to bargaining in good faith and have put forward a fair and responsible proposal that maintains Brigham nurses’ market-leading compensation, preserves meaningful wage growth and competitive benefits, and balances those investments with the long-term financial sustainability of our system,” the hospital said in a statement given to press.

The hospital has previously said it has found agreements with the union on several issues. However, the union has previously said that talks stalled in mid-August and reiterated Thursday that it still is seeking limits on the use of temporary nurses, more affordable health insurance benefits and “a meaningful cost-of-living wage increase” that includes a differential for nurses floating between units.

MGB is the largest private employer in Massachusetts with roughly 85,000 workers and $22.8 billion in annual revenue, making it among the country’s largest nonprofit health systems. Financial results released last month outlined a $15 million operating income (0.1% operating margin) across nine months of its ongoing fiscal year, up from a $44 million operating loss (-0.3% operating margin), though its nine-month bottom line including nonoperating gains like investment returns was $1.9 billion. Early last year saw the organization undertake the largest layoffs in its history, when it cut about 1,500 workers.

The union has pointed to MGB’s bottom line (nearly $2.4 billion across fiscal 2025), substantial total assets ($35.8 billion) and the compensation of executives (almost $9.2 million for CEO Anne Klibanski, M.D.) in its calls for stronger contracts.

#5734. Latin America EV Sales Report: With Over 200,000 Units Sold in Q3, EVs Now Stand at 12% Market Share!

Through 2026, EVs have gained significant momentum all over the world (safe for the US), and Latin America has been no exception. Sales grew by almost 140% in the third quarter, and clock in at a very healthy 120% growth through 2026, bringing the yearly total to more than half a million units. If this trend continues, it’s all but certain we will surpass 700,000 units by the end of the year, and perhaps even get to 800,000.

Another interesting bit of trivia is that sales reached 220,000 units in the third quarter, not too far behind the USA’s 266,000. In theory, this means it should be possible for LatAm to surpass total US EV sales as early as Q1 2027 … though, I would be much happier if the USA’s market starts growing strongly again and thus Latin America cannot get ahead.

Now, to be fair, the US is much more BEV-heavy (242,000 units sold, vs 127,000 in LatAm), whereas Latin America prefers PHEVs to a higher degree (93,000 units sold vs 44,000 in the US), but, still, these are impressive results for a region overall much poorer than the US, and with a vehicle market around a third of the size. For over a decade, it was the richest countries in the world that led EV adoption, but — as many of us predicted on this very site — that has now changed.

As mentioned earlier, total EV sales reached 220,000 units, surpassing for the first time the 200,000 mark and growing a healthy 140% YoY, and a strong 17% from Q2. BEVs grew faster than PHEVs (146% vs 130%), and thus now represent 57.5% of all EV sales in the region, slightly below the 58% result for Q2.

Market share grew to 12%, up from 10.7% in Q2 and 5.5% in Q3 last year, a pretty strong result. This brought market share above 10% through 2026, 5.9% BEV and 4.3% PHEV.

Latin America’s overall vehicle market is growing at rates of around 10% annually, but thanks to strong EV growth, combustion-based powertrains (HEV, MHEV and ICEV) are stagnant: they fell by 3.7% last quarter, and barely grew by 3.1% this one, meaning it’s very likely that we’re reaching “Peak Combustion” in Latin America and the market will only go down from 2027 onwards.

Sales wise, we have a pretty stable list, with Brazil being the unsurprising winner, followed by Mexico and Colombia, just as in Q2. Uruguay follows, but then we have a new rising star: Ecuador, which nearly reached 5,000 BEVs sold last quarter! Costa Rica, Chile, and Argentina close the top 8 and make up all the countries with over 1.000 quarterly BEV sales.

PHEV sales are much more varied, though. Brazil, of course, leads again, but following come Mexico and Argentina, with Colombia in 4th place and Ecuador in 5th.

Market share: again, we have a pretty constant list, with the first 8 positions unchanged. Uruguay, unsurprisingly, leads the region with a very strong 50.7% EV market share (45.7% BEV), followed by Costa Rica, Colombia, Ecuador, and Brazil. Notable mention to Paraguay, the sixth country in our region to reach 10% EV market share through a quarter, but in this case thanks to PHEVs.

This has been an eventful year due to Donald’s dubious defense decisions, but even as high oil prices have been driving massive EV adoption and/or massive ICEV crashes all over the world, I feel the situation in Latin America isn’t as clear cut.

In the US and Europe, fuel prices have gone up by around 40–50%, at least in the case of gasoline. Now, prices have gone up similarly in some countries in Latin America, including Panama, Paraguay and Perú, but in many others, like Brazil, Colombia and Mexico, it has barely moved, either because of significant subsidies — direct or indirect — to maintain prices, or because it was already expensive before the war and the government did not make any adjustments to its price.

One would think that the countries most affected by high fuel prices would be at the forefront of the EV transition, but no: the largest increases in EV sales only partially track gasoline prices. For example: Panama and Perú are still lagging behind the region despite having the highest increase in the region (>50% in both cases), whereas Colombia and Brazil are sprinting ahead despite relatively stable fuel prices. What gives?

The answer, I believe, is linked to EV prices and how they compare with their ICEV competition. Yes, I know the TCO is a very important metric, but evidence in our markets point to the sticker price being the main driver of adoption. The cases of Brazil and Colombia on one hand, and Peru and Panama on the other, exemplify this very well:

Brazil and Colombia have had pretty stable fuel prices, up around 10% or less since the war started, yet both have booming markets, up 160% and 190%, respectively, with EV market share getting close to 20%. Meanwhile, Panama and Peru have seen gasoline prices spike over 50% from their pre-war costs, yet the former only showed a meager 57% growth in September, and the latter, though clocking in at a more impressive 270% YoY, remains at a disappointing 1.3% market share.

The main difference has to do with the nature of the market. In Brazil and Colombia, combustion vehicles are relatively expensive — in no small part due to tariffs to protect local industry — and EVs have effectively reached price parity with their combustion counterparts. Meanwhile, in Panama and Per,u EVs are just as cheap if not cheaper than in Brazil or Colombia, but combustion cars are significantly cheaper, with some entry-level models at or below USD$10.,00. This makes customers hesitant to try the new technologies by the simple logic that even if the EV will save a lot of money in the long run, $6,000 will buy a lot of gas.

And in Peru, this is particularly relevant insofar as gas-mobiles from Chinese brands are very popular. Changan, Jetour, Geely, and JAC together account for 20% of the Peruvian market largely thanks to their hyper-affordable combustion cars, and since the Chinese gas-mobile market is collapsing, it’s likely these brands would rather keep it like this for a few more months so they can move some of the inventory they won’t be able to sell at home before betting it all on EVs.

In general, this tracks for most markets, where EV prices compared to traditional combustion cars are probably the most relevant factor to keep track of. And of course, fuel prices do have an influence, but it seems it’s rather limited compared to, for example, what we’re seeing in Europe.

But the lessons are clear: Want to improve EV sales? Either make them cheaper, or make gas-mobiles more expensive.

At the beginning of this year, I was hopeful we would see 10% market share in the fourth quarter, normally the highest in the year. We went past that in Q2, and at 12%, we’re sitting far beyond what I considered feasible only 10 months ago.

Yet, there’s still a long path ahead. Aside from the 5 leading markets, we’re yet to see a country getting consistent BEV market share above 5%, and several large markets — Chile, Argentina, and Mexico — are still lagging. PHEVs have raised the bar in several countries, Paraguay most important of all, but we would rather see more BEVs.

This is not to be overtly pessimistic. The results so far are great, much better than we would’ve expected even a year ago. But as things improve, the bar rises, and I’m now waiting to see the moment when we will see 20% market share (Q3 2027?) or when e-truck sales will start to ramp up (2027? 2028?).

Passionate for all things Latin American, I’ve been closely following the energy and mobility transitions since they started to become present south of the equator.
