#5715. Cancer Vaccines Show Promise. But We Have More Work to Do.

— A look at how individualized cancer vaccines may fit into a complex treatment landscape

The controversy surrounding the premature disclosure of Moderna and Merck's mRNA melanoma vaccine results risks overshadowing a more consequential clinical discussion: how individualized cancer vaccines might fit into an increasingly effective and increasingly complex treatment landscape.

The results are very encouraging. Reducing recurrence and distant metastases by adding a treatment with a new mechanism to an effective checkpoint inhibitor represent meaningful progress. Our work now is to determine which patients benefit, how vaccination should be sequenced with other treatments, and whether its promise extends beyond melanoma.

In INTerpath-001, which randomized 1,137 patients with completely resected stage IIB–IV melanoma, results presented at ESMO showed 2-year recurrence-free survival of 82.2% with the mRNA-based cancer vaccine intismeran autogene plus pembrolizumab (Keytruda) versus 70% with placebo plus pembrolizumab. The absolute difference was 12.2 percentage points; the hazard ratio was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.45-0.75). At a median follow-up of 24.6 months, an overall survival benefit had not been demonstrated.

Preventing recurrence has clinical value. It can spare patients further treatment and morbidity. But not all patients benefited from the intervention, and these findings do not establish efficacy across other cancers.

The biological rationale behind intismeran autogene is compelling. Personalized mRNA vaccines encode tumor-specific neoantigens that antigen-presenting cells process and present to prime and expand tumor-reactive T cells. PD-1 blockade complements this response by reducing inhibitory signaling that limits T-cell activity. Vaccination may therefore broaden tumor-directed immunity while checkpoint inhibition supports its function. INTerpath-001 demonstrates the benefit of adding vaccination to pembrolizumab; without a vaccine-only arm, it cannot formally establish synergy.

This approach brings together tumor sequencing, computational antigen selection, mRNA delivery, and immunotherapy. Yet a predicted neoantigen is not necessarily an effective immune target. Translational studies must clarify which responses control the cancer clones responsible for recurrence.

The vaccine discussion also needs to account for progress in neoadjuvant immunotherapy. In SWOG S1801, beginning pembrolizumab before surgery improved event-free survival compared with administering it entirely afterward. In NADINA, neoadjuvant nivolumab-ipilimumab followed by surgery and response-directed postoperative therapy improved event-free survival compared with surgery followed by nivolumab (Opdivo).

These advances make sequencing a central research question. Could vaccination improve outcomes after neoadjuvant immunotherapy? Might patients without a major pathological response have the greatest need? Conversely, could patients with a major response avoid additional treatment?

INTerpath-001 does not answer these questions. Nor can cross-trial comparisons, as populations, endpoints, and treatment strategies differ. The neoadjuvant question is particularly relevant to patients with clinically apparent, resectable stage III disease; it should not obscure the vaccine findings in other patients represented in the trial.

We need studies that integrate advances in treatment rather than simply accumulate postoperative therapies. Residual disease after checkpoint inhibition also does not necessarily imply vaccine sensitivity. That hypothesis requires testing.

Beyond melanoma, our optimism must remain tempered by the evidence. Tumors differ in antigen availability, antigen presentation, immune infiltration, and mechanisms of immune suppression. Still, early findings justify investigation and enthusiasm. A phase I pancreatic cancer study demonstrated persistent vaccine-induced T-cell responses in some patients receiving an individualized mRNA vaccine alongside atezolizumab and chemotherapy. Immune responders had longer recurrence-free survival than nonresponders.

This establishes biological activity, not that vaccination improves outcomes in pancreatic cancer. The study was small, lacked a randomized control group, and compared patients according to their immune response. A randomized trial is evaluating the combination more rigorously.

Patient selection deserves similar discipline. Pathological response and circulating tumor DNA are attractive candidates for refining postoperative decisions. But identifying patients at higher risk of recurrence is different from identifying those more likely to benefit from vaccination. Biomarker-guided treatment strategies require prospective evaluation.

Delivery is another clinical endpoint in practice. In INTerpath-001, vaccine production was successful for more than 99% of patients assigned to intismeran, an encouraging feasibility result. Median time to the first vaccine dose was 64 days. That interval is not simply a manufacturing-time estimate, but it makes treatment coordination -- and the feasibility of preoperative vaccination -- important research questions.

Safety also requires attention. Grade 3-5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 14.2% of patients receiving intismeran plus pembrolizumab versus 13.4% of those receiving pembrolizumab alone. However, all-cause adverse events led to discontinuation of any study drug in 16.6% versus 9.5%, respectively. Similar rates of severe treatment-related toxicity do not establish an identical treatment burden.

Regulators must evaluate manufacturing consistency alongside efficacy and safety. Clinicians need durable outcomes, patient-reported quality of life, and practical delivery data. Health systems must determine whether treatment is feasible and affordable beyond specialized centers.

As an oncologist working in clinical development and global cancer care, I would place access within the development agenda from the beginning. Adequate tissue, sequencing capacity, production infrastructure, and coverage and reimbursement will determine who benefits.

Personalized cancer vaccines could become an important component of perioperative treatment. Their greatest contribution may come through careful integration with checkpoint inhibition, response assessment, and better patient selection. Our responsibility is to translate an encouraging result into longer and better lives, while avoiding unnecessary treatment, toxicity, and financial burden.

#5714. What Is a Great Google Quality Real Estate Score: A Comprehensive Guide

Navigating the world of Google Ads can be challenging, especially in an industry as competitive as real estate. One term you've probably heard in relation to Google Ads is "Quality Score." This score is crucial to how your ads perform and how much they cost. But what does it mean for realtors, and what constitutes a great Google Quality Real Estate Score? Let's dive in.

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

A high-Quality Score is beneficial for several reasons:

Improving your Quality Score is all about relevance and user experience. Here are some strategies:

A high Google Ads Quality Score can be a strong asset for realtors. It not only helps you rank higher and pay less for clicks but also ensures your ads are shown to the most relevant audiences. However, remember that Quality Score is just one piece of the puzzle. You should also consider other factors like your bidding strategy and overall account performance to create a successful Google Ads campaign.

With continuous effort and strategic planning, you can optimize your Quality Score and ultimately generate more leads for your real estate business.

#5713. AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis

An artificial intelligence model called REDMOD can identify extremely subtle changes in pancreatic tissue that may signal cancer long before the disease becomes visible to doctors or conventional imaging technology. According to research published online in the journal Gut, the system can detect early signs of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.

Researchers believe this technology could help transform pancreatic cancer detection by identifying the disease at a much earlier stage (stage 0), when treatment is more likely to succeed. Instead of receiving a diagnosis after the cancer has progressed to an advanced, potentially terminal stage, patients might have an opportunity to begin treatment while the disease is still treatable.

Although REDMOD outperformed experienced radiologists in the study, more research is necessary before it can be introduced into routine medical care. In particular, the scientists emphasize the need to test the system in patients at high risk, including those experiencing unexplained weight loss or recently diagnosed diabetes.

Why Pancreatic Cancer Is So Difficult to Detect Early

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a low survival rate, largely because it is often discovered only after the disease has advanced. Early pancreatic cancer typically produces few noticeable symptoms, and the changes it causes in pancreatic tissue can be too subtle to detect through standard medical imaging. The cancer can also progress rapidly, making timely diagnosis especially important.

To address these challenges, researchers created an artificial intelligence framework known as Radiomics-based Early Detection MODel (REDMOD). The system analyzes extremely fine patterns in the texture of pancreatic tissue, known as radiomics (radiomics), that are not readily visible on conventional computed tomography (CT) scans.

REDMOD also automatically identifies and outlines the pancreas, separating it from nearby organs and tissues. This process eliminates the need for specialists to manually trace the organ's boundaries, reducing the inconsistencies that can arise when different people perform the task.

AI Finds Hidden Cancer Signals Years Before Diagnosis

To evaluate the system, the researchers examined abdominal CT scans from 219 patients treated at multiple hospitals. At the time of their scans, experienced radiologists had found no evidence of pancreatic cancer. However, every patient in this group was subsequently diagnosed with the disease.

The scans had been taken at different intervals before diagnosis. For 87 patients (40%), the images were obtained 3 to 12 months earlier. Another 76 patients (35%) had been scanned 12 to 24 months before diagnosis, while 56 (25%) had undergone imaging more than 24 months earlier (up to around 3 years). In nearly two thirds (64%) of the patients, the cancer developed in the head of the pancreas.

The researchers compared these images with CT scans from 1243 people who remained free of pancreatic cancer for up to three years afterward. The comparison group was matched according to age, sex, and the dates of their scans.

Patients who eventually developed pancreatic cancer had an average age of 69, with ages ranging from 34 to 88. Those in the comparison group were 64 years old on average, with the same age range of 34 to 88.

REDMOD successfully identified subtle imaging signatures associated with pancreatic cancer an average of 475 days before patients received their clinical diagnoses. These early warning signs had previously gone undetected during routine radiological assessments.

"This temporal window holds profound significance, as attaining such early detection would substantially augment the probability of cure and improved survival," highlight the researchers.

"In fact, modelling studies indicate that increasing the proportion of localized [pancreatic ductal carcinomas] from 10% to 50% would more than double survival rates, thereby underscoring that the timing of diagnosis is the single most critical determinant of survival outcomes," they add.

The results also showed that REDMOD was substantially better than experienced radiologists at recognizing early cancer signals.

The AI achieved a sensitivity of 73%, compared with 39% for radiologists. Sensitivity measures how effectively a diagnostic method identifies people who actually have the disease, rather than overlooking genuine cases.

The difference was even more pronounced when researchers examined scans taken more than two years before the patients were diagnosed. In these cases, REDMOD achieved a detection rate of 68%, nearly three times the 23% recorded by radiologists.

The researchers also assessed how well the system could recognize scans from people without pancreatic cancer. In an independent group of 539 patients from several hospitals, REDMOD correctly classified just over 81% of scans as cancer free. It performed even better on the publicly available US National Institutes of Health NIH-PCT dataset (80 patients), correctly identifying 87.5% as free of pancreatic cancer.

Additional testing suggested that the early warning signs detected by REDMOD were consistent over time. When the researchers analyzed scans taken from the same patients several months apart, the system produced matching results in 90 to 92% of cases. This consistency strengthened the evidence that the AI was identifying meaningful changes associated with the disease.

Could AI Transform Early Pancreatic Cancer Detection?

Despite the promising findings, the researchers caution that several questions remain unanswered. One limitation is that the study population did not include a sufficiently diverse range of ethnic backgrounds, which could affect how well the technology performs across different populations.

The system must also undergo prospective testing, particularly among people at increased risk of pancreatic cancer, before researchers can determine whether it will be effective in everyday clinical practice.

Even with these limitations, the findings suggest that AI could eventually help doctors identify pancreatic cancer while it is still at a much more treatable stage, potentially improving survival for patients who would otherwise receive a late diagnosis.

The researchers conclude: "This study validates REDMOD as a fully automated AI framework capable of identifying the imaging signatures of stage 0 [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] in normal pancreas, achieving this with substantial lead times and performance superior to expert radiologists."

They add: "While prospective validation is paramount to confirm clinical utility, the REDMOD framework represents a significant advance towards shifting the paradigm for sporadic [pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma] from a late-stage symptomatic diagnosis to proactive pre-clinical interception, offering tangible hope for improving outcomes in this challenging disease."

Hinge Health is seeing early traction with its migraine and gastrointestinal care programs as it pushes beyond musculoskeletal care and builds a broader, multi-condition platform.

But the company's core MSK business remains the engine fueling its robust growth.

"Our vision has always been to automate the delivery of care using technology to close the gap between the care people need and the care they actually receive. We're now applying that same approach and the same trusted relationships with employers and partners in neurology and gastrointestinal care," Daniel Perez, Hinge Health co-founder and CEO, told analysts and investors on the third-quarter earnings call Monday. "We're not starting from scratch in each new category. We're extending a platform that's already proven into conditions that are often connected to the ones we already treat. We believe that's a fundamentally different and more powerful way to expand than what other companies in our space are attempting."

During a Q&A with analysts and investors on the earnings call, Perez asserted, "We’re not taking our eye off the ball in MSK. I think we’re actually widening our lead on MSK … But it’s allowing us to expand into other areas as well."

In the third quarter, the company posted $235 million in revenue, up 52% from $154 million a year ago, and above its guidance range of $223 million to $225 million. The company posted third-quarter adjusted earnings of 66 cents per share, exceeding Wall Street analysts' estimates of 60 cents per share. Hinge Health's non-GAAP income from operations increased 154% to $77.2 million in the third quarter.

Hinge Health, which launched in late 2014 and went public in May 2025, developed software combined with AI to automate physical therapy services for joint and muscle health. The company has designed its platform to address a broad spectrum of MSK care, including acute injury, chronic pain and post-surgical rehabilitation. To address the automation of care, Hinge has developed AI-powered motion tracking technology, a proprietary FDA-cleared wearable device called Enso, and an AI-supported care team to deliver scalable and personalized MSK care.

The company reported strong client growth, with 3,270 clients as of September 30, up 28% from a year ago. Last twelve months (LTM) calculated billings increased 54% year-over-year to $960 million as of September 30, compared to $624 million during Q3 2025.

The company also benefited from strong operational efficiency as it reported a gross margin of 87% in Q3, compared to 82% during the same quarter a year ago.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $113 million, representing a 51% free cash flow margin. The company ended the September quarter with total cash and equivalents of $359 million.

Based on strong Q3 and year-to-date results, Hinge Health boosted its 2026 outlook, now expecting full-year revenue to reach between $879 million and $881 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 50% at the midpoint. That compares to the prior revenue target of $856 million to $860 million. The company now projects non-GAAP income from operations to be between $266 million and $268 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 123% and non-GAAP operating margin of 30% at the midpoint.

Core MSK is still the company's largest revenue contributor by a wide margin, Perez noted, and that business is growing robustly. "We expect it to remain that way for years to come; the opportunity at MSK remains massively underpenetrated," Perez said.

"The MSK opportunity is still enormous. Musculoskeletal conditions are among the leading drivers of disability and healthcare spend in the United States, and the vast majority of people in America still don't have access to a digital MSK solution," Perez said during the call.

"We built something that works clinically, commercially, and economically, and we're still in the early innings of penetrating that market. We are the undisputed leader in this space, and we estimate 88% of lives within our markets are yet to be won, leaving a long runway for growth. That alone is a multi-year growth opportunity," he said.

The company is building on top of that MSK care foundation as it expands into migraine care and gastrointestinal care. Hinge acquired GI startup Cylinder Health in August for $105 million in cash.

The company's client base is up almost 30% year-over-year for its MSK care program and roughly 40% for its new GI Care Program since the acquisition announcement of Cylinder Health in August, Perez noted.

The company expects to make more acquisitions and is even looking at hardware acquisitions, Perez said. "I think too many technology companies, especially in healthcare, focus exclusively on software, but I absolutely firmly believe you will not automate care delivery without also investing in hardware. And we've shown we're pretty good at hardware," he said as the company internally developed its Enso wearable device.

Perez told Bloomberg last month that the company was interested in hardware that can augment virtual care.

"We will build organically first and use M&A when it accelerates our timeline. And our acquisitions, particularly in hardware, have historically been small tuck-ins of technology in a team, and then you build it out into something much larger," he added.

Looking at the company's new care programs, Perez called out notable early results from Hinge's migraine program, which is still in early access: 23% reduction in monthly migraine days, 28% reduction in migraine duration, equivalent to roughly five hours and just over half of surveyed members achieved a clinically meaningful improvement.

"We're also seeing a meaningful reduction in monthly prescription use days, which matters both for members and for the clients paying for their care," Perez said.

More than 800 clients, representing 9 million lives, now have access to the migraine program, approximately double the previous quarter, according to management. The migraine program was announced in May.

For the GI care business, Hinge Health is taking Cylinder's existing program and building it into the same app and care infrastructure it uses for MSK and migraine. The company is targeting summer 2027 for the fully integrated product. Meaningful revenue contribution should emerge particularly in 2028, after Hinge gets a fuller sales cycle with the integrated product, Perez noted.

Hinge Health sees an opportunity to offer health plans and employers one integrated care platform that covers multiple health conditions rather than separate point solutions.

Nearly one in two people with GI conditions also have MSK pain, and 70% of people withmigraine also have a GI condition, Perez noted.

"GI cost has been a growing pain point for employers and health plans, especially with the growth of GLP-1s, given GI side effects are so common, and our employer clients are very grateful for taking this on," he said during the call.

Hinge Health had a strong selling season in Q3, according to Aaryn Pure, Hinge Health's chief commercial officer, with three new Fortune 15 clients. "We've already received verbal agreements on more lives this year than we closed in all of last year, and last year was a record-breaking sales year for adding eligible lives," Pure noted.

More than 10 million lives across over 800 clients have access to multiple Hinge products, he said.

Small and midsize businesses are becoming an important growth channel for the company, even though Hinge began investing in that market just a year ago. Through Q3, Hinge Health closed nearly 1 million SMB lives, "demonstrating we're not just winning at the top of the market, we're adding clients across every size tier," Pure said on the call.

He also noted that some health plan and third-party administrator (TPA) partners are implementing or considering arrangements where Hinge Health is automatically embedded or offered on an opt-out basis in their SMB book of business.

"Being the first-mover preferred partner is allowing us to capture that market," Pure said.

The company also announced Monday that Jim Pursley will step down as president, effective January 1, and will join Hinge Health's board of directors. Following this transition, Pure will lead the commercial organization, the company said.

In an analyst note, Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Hinge Health demonstrates "market leadership with significant advantages both on the product and go-to-market fronts."

"With a nearly 150% increase in shares YTD, HNGE now trades at approximately 11 times our 2027 adjusted gross profit, a premium to mature, high-margin, growth-oriented healthcare IT peers. Still, at these levels, we believe the stock presents a compelling long-term risk/reward and see continued growth momentum and upside to operating income and free cash flow estimates," Daniels wrote.

#5711. Why Are Medical Students Learning About Physician Unions?

— Brian Muthyala, MD, MPH, weighs the promise and pitfalls of collective action

Medical students are taught how poverty, access to care, and other systemic factors affect patients' health, but many struggle with a fundamental question: What can one physician realistically do about problems that extend far beyond the exam room?

At the University of Minnesota Medical School in Minneapolis, Brian Muthyala, MD, MPH, teaches second-year students about building collective power -- including physician unionization -- as one potential approach to addressing systemic challenges in healthcare.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Muthyala discusses why he introduced the course, how physicians can advocate for patients beyond individual clinical encounters, and why he believes unionization holds promise but is not without risks.

The following is a transcript of this video:

I don't think unionization is a panacea. I don't think it's a silver bullet, and it has its own risks.

So I started teaching this course and it's built on the idea that collective problems require collective solutions. So I'm the director of our social medicine thread in the medical school at the University of Minnesota. And so what I teach is around all of the nonbiological reasons that one person might be sick.

And in the context of many conversations over the medical students' first 2 years, they get to this point where they recognize that poverty, low socioeconomic status, a history of experiencing structural racism, you name it, all of these are sort of large collective problems. And many students say, "Well, what am I supposed to do about that? I'm just one person and I need to learn how to take care of pneumonia and heart attacks and rheumatologic conditions. I need to learn all these things, and I've got to deal with this too. What am I supposed to do?"

And the session is really two parts. And so the first is a webinar that's sort of a conversation around what are different ways historically that physicians have built collective power. We talk about things like mutual aid. We talk about things like community-based participation. And then one of the things we talk about is the history of unionization by physicians historically. The second part of that series is I brought a panel of mostly physicians, but also labor organizers as well, to talk about the issue of physician unionization -- challenges, pitfalls, all of those things as one approach that's imperfect certainly, but one approach to building the collective voice of physicians to try to solve large societal or collective problems that exist.

Historically, the way I was taught physician advocacy was, well, if you've got a problem with something, write a letter to your senator, go testify at the Capitol. And that feels unreachable to a lot of students. They're like, "I'm really busy right now. And then when I'm a physician, I have 20-minute appointments. I've got all this paperwork. I've got all this stuff to do. That feels really inaccessible."

We don't get to ignore it as physicians. As physicians, we're sort of stewards of a community trust and it's our responsibility to understand these issues to the best of our ability and address them to the best of our ability -- and that doesn't mean quitting our day job and going to the Capitol or whatever. And so I give them this sort of pyramid of approach and the first level is understanding the problem. So reading about it, understanding the history, learning.

The second is how do I start to communicate interpersonally with patients around these issues as they impact? How does access to care affect the patient that I'm sitting in front of? The next is how do I understand my own institution's support around these issues? What does my clinic do to help somebody sign up for insurance if they just lost Medicaid, whatever that may be. Because every system is going to be different in terms of what resources they have. And the last is a policy level. You get to choose which level you want to approach these issues.

We've seen a corporatization of healthcare delivery in the last 25 years. If you want to have a seat at the table, we have to build a system that will allow you to operate against and oftentimes push against large corporate interests, which I and others, and I think many students identify as something that puts patients at risk. And ultimately that's what this comes down to is I think unionization can be -- I don't know if it has always been -- can be one way to elevate the needs of patients to a level in which they can be advocated for. And I think physicians are responding to the corporatization of medical care.

I say this in the class: I am nervous about physician unionization. Historically, physician groups have not been unions, but physician groups have been professional societies, so like the American Medical Association [AMA] as an example. My worry about physician unions are the same worries that I have around historical physician groups. The AMA was against the initial legislation that brought forward Medicare and Medicaid in this country. The AMA, again, historically at its inception did not allow for nonwhite physicians to join its ranks.

And so the history of physicians joining their collective voice is complicated and physicians are not a homogeneous group. In fact, I think we're a very heterogeneous group. Will unions be able to focus a large heterogeneous group's energies, privilege, power towards the betterment of patients is a question that I don't think has been answered. And I think rightfully should be questioned if it's possible.

I'm an optimist by my nature and I think that the more voices that are at a table that are not representative of corporate entities is a good one. And so I think physician unions have the potential and possibility of really advocating for significant change for the betterment of patients, but that remains to be seen at this point.

#5710. Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases

Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5709. The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure

New research suggests that exercising just once or twice a week may be enough to maintain some of the blood pressure benefits gained from regular physical activity, at least over a short period. However, people who continue exercising three times weekly may experience larger and more sustained improvements.

The findings, published in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, suggest that even a single weekly session of isometric exercise could help people preserve improvements in blood pressure when they cannot commit to a more frequent workout schedule.

Isometric exercise involves tightening muscles while holding the body in a fixed position for several minutes. Common examples include wall squats, planks, and handgrip exercises.

Earlier research has found that isometric training can lower blood pressure more effectively than other types of exercise, sometimes producing reductions comparable to or greater than those achieved with certain medications. However, researchers have not fully understood how often these exercises need to be performed to maintain their cardiovascular benefits.

To investigate, researchers enrolled 100 adults whose average age was 37.4 years. Participants had systolic blood pressure ranging from normal to high-normal levels (120-140 mmHg) and did not regularly participate in structured exercise programs.

Under expert guidelines, systolic blood pressure between 130 and 139 mmHg falls into the "high-normal" category, which warrants specific lifestyle recommendations from healthcare professionals. None of the participants had been diagnosed with hypertension.

To qualify, volunteers had to be free of injuries and illnesses, have no current or previous use of blood pressure medication, and be nonsmokers. They also had to consume no more than 14 units of alcohol per week.

Participants were randomly assigned to five groups. One served as a control group, while the other four began the same four-week exercise program at home, focusing on isometric movements involving the lower body.

The training consisted of four wall squat holds per session, with two minutes of seated recovery between each hold. Participants completed this routine three times weekly during the first four weeks.

After this initial training period, the four exercise groups followed different schedules for another four weeks. One continued with three weekly sessions, another reduced its frequency to twice weekly, and a third performed the exercises only once a week. The fourth group stopped training altogether.

Researchers evaluated blood pressure, heart rate, and additional measures of cardiovascular function at the beginning of the experiment and again after four and eight weeks.

Even One Weekly Workout Helped Preserve Blood Pressure Benefits

After the first four weeks, all four exercise groups showed significant improvements compared with the control group. These included reductions in systolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart contracts, and diastolic blood pressure, which measures pressure when the heart relaxes. Mean arterial pressure, a measure of average blood pressure throughout the cardiac cycle, also decreased significantly.

These initial results were consistent with earlier studies demonstrating the blood pressure benefits of isometric exercise. However, after participants switched to their assigned maintenance schedules, the groups no longer showed statistically significant differences in diastolic blood pressure.

By the end of the eight-week study, participants exercising just once or twice weekly had maintained significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure compared with the control group. Neither schedule maintained a statistically significant improvement in diastolic blood pressure.

The greatest benefits appeared among participants who continued performing wall squats three times per week. Their systolic blood pressure fell by an average of 13.73 mmHg (-13.73 mmHg) from the beginning of the study.

By comparison, the twice-weekly group experienced an average reduction of 6.95 mmHg, while participants exercising once a week recorded a decrease of 6.56 mmHg.

Those who maintained the three-session schedule also preserved improvements in other cardiovascular measurements, including total peripheral resistance (an indication that blood vessels have narrowed) and heart rate variability.

Stopping Exercise Caused Blood Pressure Benefits to Fade

The results also revealed what happened when participants stopped exercising completely.

Those who discontinued wall squats after the initial four weeks experienced a reversal of their earlier blood pressure improvements. By the end of the study, their readings were no longer statistically different from those of the control group.

This finding suggests that maintaining some level of regular isometric exercise may be important for preserving the cardiovascular improvements gained during training.

However, the researchers emphasized that the maintenance phase lasted only four weeks. Additional studies following participants for longer periods will be needed to determine whether less frequent training can preserve these benefits over months or years.

"The study demonstrates that while lower frequency isometric exercise training may be sufficient to maintain blood pressure reductions over the short term, higher frequencies are required to preserve these benefits and the associated vascular and cardiac autonomic adaptations," the researchers write.

"The study offers evidence that lower frequency isometric exercise training can help maintain short-term blood pressure reductions, providing a pragmatic option for individuals with limited time or adherence challenges."

#5708. CD38-Targeted Immuno-PET Tracer Can Detect Overlooked Multiple Myeloma

— "While no imaging modality is perfect, this adds a new tool," says researcher

A novel CD38-targeted immuno-PET tracer could help detect multiple myeloma in some patients with no signs of disease, according to results from a phase II trial.

While there was no overall difference in disease detection with CD38-targeted zirconium 89 (89Zr) deferoxamine (DFO)-daratumumab PET/CT versus standard-of-care fluorine 18 (18F)-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT (43% vs 47%, P=0.81), both scans identified multiple lesions not visible on the other, reported Gary A. Ulaner, MD, PhD, of the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, and colleagues in Radiology.

For example, multiple myeloma was demonstrated in 13% of patients only with 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab PET/CT and 17% of patients only with 18F-FDG PET/CT.

Moreover, the CD38-targeted immuno-PET tracer identified more sites of disease than standard imaging in 28% of patients, while 18F-FDG PET/CT identified more sites of disease in 22%. The two imaging approaches detected a similar amount of disease in the remaining patients.

"This study demonstrates that immuno-PET targeting CD38 can identify, localize, and quantify myeloma, which is overlooked by FDG PET in many patients," Ulaner told MedPage Today. "This allows oncologists to optimally stage, target, and treat disease."

"While no imaging modality is perfect, this adds a new tool for the care of patients with multiple myeloma," he added.

In a press release, co-author C. Ola Landgren, MD, PhD, of the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, noted that "if we are going to cure multiple myeloma, we need two things. One, we need really effective medicines. Second, we need to be able to make sure there is no disease left behind after these treatments."

"We are developing new and better technology designed to see where the disease is and make sure we are not missing it," he said. "We show that you can successfully find much more disease. It's a more sensitive and more precise technology, and we have very strong proof of principle that it works and that it's meaningful."

In an editorial accompanying the study, Peter Choyke, MD, of the National Cancer Institute, observed that neither of the two agents detected more than half of the disease present in patients with histologically confirmed disease.

However, while those results may be "disappointing from a clinical perspective, there are several reasons for optimism," he wrote.

Choyke suggested that when combined with highly sensitive liquid biopsies, molecular imaging "might detect ... early disease that would otherwise be missed with conventional imaging and bone marrow biopsy."

In addition, he noted that 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab as a molecular imaging agent is based on daratumumab (Darzalex), which is an actual treatment for multiple myeloma, "so a positive scan implies the drug might be effective."

Ulaner and colleagues noted that while treatment for multiple myeloma has significantly improved over the past two decades, detection of multiple myeloma disease burden remains "suboptimal."

They pointed out that standard-of-care 18F-FDG PET/CT assessment is based on radiolabeled glucose uptake and has limited utility in patients with plasma cell disorders, since myeloma cells may have low glucose uptake. Thus, disease may be undetected with the standard imaging in 30% to 50% of patients with established bone lesions.

The idea behind immuno-PET imaging is that it integrates the target specificity of monoclonal antibodies like daratumumab with the sensitivity and quantitative power of PET, allowing for whole-body mapping of tumor and immune biomarkers.

This prospective, two-center trial was conducted between March 2022 and July 2025, and included 60 participants (median age 63 years, 53% women) who had previously pathologically proven CD38-positive multiple myeloma; had at least one tumor lesion visualized on CT, MRI, or 18F-FDG PET/CT performed within 90 days of protocol enrollment; had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group score of 0-2; and were planned for first-line or a new line of myeloma therapy.

Ulaner and team reported that there were no severe adverse events with 89Zr-DFO-daratumumab, while non-severe adverse events occurred in 5% of participants during non-radiolabeled daratumumab administration.

Humana and athenahealth are expanding electronic prior authorizations nationwide in a newly announced collaboration.

In June 2025, insurers nationwide—including Humana—agreed to take steps to reform prior authorization, including supporting electronic prior authorizations.

#5705. The Power of Schema Markup: A Comprehensive Guide for Real Estate Agents

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

Implementing Schema Markup for Real Estate

#5704. Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging

Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.

The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.

The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.

"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.

Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike

Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.

To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.

Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.

Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..

A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation

Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.

The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.

In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.

Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:

Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells

The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.

The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.

When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.

Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.

These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.

Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:

A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research

Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.

The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.

Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.

The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.

By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.

#5703. Brain Health Linked With Longer Lifetime Estrogen Exposure

— Menopausal hormone therapy tied to lower cerebral small vessel disease burden, study shows

Women with higher lifetime estrogen exposure had less cerebrovascular pathology, a cohort study in Sweden showed.

A longer reproductive span was associated with 8% lower odds of having two or more signs of cerebral small vessel disease (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86-0.99), reported Anna Marseglia, PhD, of the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and co-authors.

Menopausal hormone therapy was also linked with lower cerebral small vessel disease burden (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.20-0.81) and with increasing white matter integrity (ß=0.28, 95% CI 0.06-0.50), Marseglia and colleagues wrote in Neurology.

Among APOE4 carriers only, menopausal hormone therapy was associated with greater cortical thickness in brain regions typically affected by Alzheimer's disease (β=0.38, 95% CI 0.01-0.76).

Women who used oral contraceptives earlier in life and menopausal hormone therapy later had the lowest small vessel disease burden (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12-0.83) and the greatest white matter integrity (β=0.45, 95% CI 0.12-0.78), the researchers said.

"What was particularly striking was that the most favorable vascular brain health was observed among women who had used oral contraceptives during their reproductive years and later received menopausal hormone therapy. This suggests that hormonal factors acting across different stages of a woman's life may have cumulative associations with cerebrovascular health in older age," Marseglia said in a statement.

"While these findings do not establish cause and effect, they underscore the importance of considering women's reproductive and hormonal history when studying brain aging and dementia risk, not only in relation to Alzheimer's disease but also to vascular disease," she added.

The role of endogenous and exogenous estrogen exposure in brain health may be an opportunity to identify dementia mechanisms, observed Tracy Madsen, MD, PhD, of the University of Vermont in Burlington.

"The lifetime risk of dementia in U.S. women exceeds that of men, and recent projections suggest that by 2060, the number of incident dementia cases in women will surpass that of men by 233,000," Madsen wrote in an accompanying editorial.

The link between estrogen exposure and brain health has become more important with the FDA's recent removal of its black box warning from menopausal hormone therapy, Madsen pointed out. "Furthermore, the idea of reproductive lifespan and ovarian longevity as a potential modifiable target is a critical concept for women's health," she wrote.

Early research suggested that menopausal hormone therapy might protect against Alzheimer's and cardiovascular disease, but in 2003, the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS) reported that estrogen-plus-progestin formulations increased probable dementia risk in women ages 65 or older. The Women's Health Initiative trial also linked combined estrogen and progestin to higher breast cancer and heart disease risks, leading to black box warnings which the FDA removed in 2026.

Over time, the use of hormone replacement therapy in the U.S. declined among postmenopausal women from 26.9% in 1999 to 4.7% in 2020. The treatment is still considered controversial.

More recently, autopsy data and other research have linked estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy with reduced Alzheimer's neuropathology and lower odds of a dementia diagnosis. A large U.K. Biobank study also suggested that starting hormone replacement therapy early was associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's and dementia.

In their study, Marseglia and colleagues assessed 352 cognitively unimpaired women from the 1944 Gothenburg H70 birth cohort study who had brain MRI at age 70. Of these, 286 participated in a follow-up exam 5 years later.

The mean Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score was 29.2 at baseline, indicating normal cognitive function. About one-third (31%) of the cohort were APOE4 carriers.

Reproductive lifespan was calculated by subtracting the age at menarche from the age at menopause or oophorectomy. Study outcomes included cerebral small vessel disease, Alzheimer's-related cortical thickness, and white matter integrity. Small vessel disease burden was a composite score derived from white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, cerebral microbleeds, and perivascular spaces.

On average, women had a reproductive lifespan of 37.1 years. Most women (72.7%) reported using oral contraceptives; 60.8% reported using menopausal hormone therapy.

Longer estrogen exposure was associated with stable cortical thickness and white matter trajectories over time, the researchers said. Use of menopausal hormone therapy was linked with fewer perivascular spaces and cerebral microbleeds, they added.

Hormone exposure was reported by participants and may be subject to recall bias and misclassification, Marseglia and co-authors acknowledged. The study lacked detailed information about oral contraceptive and hormone therapy use.

#5701. Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF

Medicare Part D premiums projected to rise 50% in 2027 without plan switching: KFF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medicare beneficiaries who remain in their current stand-alone Part D drug plans could face sharply higher premiums in 2027 if they don’t switch to lower-cost plans during open enrollment, according to a KFF analysis.

The average monthly premium for stand-alone prescription drug plans, or PDPs, is projected to rise 50%, from $34 in 2026 to $51 in 2027, if current enrollees remain in the same plans, according to the analysis from KFF, an independent source for health policy research, polling and news.

The increase would widen the gap between stand-alone drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans that include prescription drug coverage. KFF projects that drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans that offer Part D coverage, or MA-PDs, will average $9 a month in 2027, compared with $51 for PDPs. The average PDP premium would rise by $17, compared with an increase of less than $2 for MA-PDs.

For Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, the average beneficiary has 28 Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans (MA-PDs) and 9 stand-alone prescription drug plans (PDPs) to choose from, with varying costs associated with these different options. KFF analysts examined premiums and cost-sharing requirements for Part D coverage in 2027 and how these costs have changed over time, based on Medicare plan landscape and benefits data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The $51 figure assumes current PDP enrollees remain in their existing plans. The actual average premium could be lower as beneficiaries switch to less expensive plans during open enrollment and new beneficiaries select coverage.

CMS projected a much smaller increase in the national average Part D premium, from $35 to $36. KFF noted that CMS, which based its estimate on September 2026 enrollment, did not explain its calculation methodology.

Among PDP enrollees who do not receive low-income subsidies, 76%, or 10.4 million people, would pay higher premiums if they keep their current plans. About 2.4 million would see their monthly premiums increase by more than $50.

That's a sharp increase from 2026, when only 38,000 enrollees faced monthly premium increases exceeding $50, according to KFF. The Trump administration’s decision to discontinue the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration after 2026 ended the additional premium subsidies that were provided to PDP sponsors and the cap on the maximum allowable monthly PDP premium increase, which was set at $50 for 2026, according to KFF analysts.

Another 4.1 million beneficiaries without low-income subsidies are enrolled in zero-premium PDPs this year, but no zero-premium PDPs will be available in 2027.

“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, said in a statement. “There are relatively low-premium PDP options, but people facing large premium increases need to take action if they want to avoid paying significantly more.”

According to KFF's analysis, if PDP enrollees who are not receiving Part D Low-Income Subsidies (LIS) keep their current plan in 2027, more than half (55%), or 7.5 million people, will pay premiums of less than $20 per month, but nearly 30%, or 3.9 million people, will pay at least $100 per month.

Average monthly premiums for the eight national PDPs are projected to range from around $6 to $204 in 2027. Among national PDPs, the two lowest-premium plans are Centene’s Wellcare Value Script Rx, an enhanced PDP with an average premium of $6.50 for 2027, up from $5.80 in 2026,  and Wellcare Classic, a basic PDP with an average premium of $10.90 for 2027, up from $8.60 in 2026, according to the analysis. The national PDPs with the highest average monthly premiums are United’s AARP Medicare Rx Preferred at $204.50, up from $126.00 in 2026, and Humana Premier Rx Plan at $137.40, up from $119.60 in 2026.

The analysis also finds that most Part D enrollees will face a deductible of several hundred dollars for drug coverage in 2027, including 85% of MA-PD enrollees, up from 80% in 2026, and virtually all PDP enrollees, 99.8%, up from 96% in 2026, based on current enrollment. The average Part D deductible in 2027 will be $643 for PDP enrollees, up from $540 in 2026,  and $489 for MA-PD enrollees, rising from $360 in 2026. The standard Part D deductible in 2027 is $700, up from $615 in 2026.

Most Part D enrollees will also face coinsurance rather than fixed copayments for preferred-brand and non-preferred drugs, potentially making their out-of-pocket costs less predictable. Virtually all PDP enrollees will face median coinsurance of 25% for preferred brands and 35% for non-preferred drugs, according to KFF.

#5700. Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease

Scientists from the University of Oxford, Newcastle University, and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust have uncovered a previously unexplained cause of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The discovery could change how doctors understand, diagnose, and treat certain forms of the condition.

The findings indicate that IBD is not simply one disease. Instead, it appears to include several biologically distinct conditions that develop through different processes in the body. Identifying these differences could make it possible to provide treatments tailored to the specific cause of each patient's illness.

In a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers examined more than 4,900 people with IBD and identified two important findings. First, some patients produce antibodies that interfere with interleukin-10 (IL-10), an essential protein that helps prevent excessive inflammation. Second, this autoimmune reaction explains how one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for IBD contributes to the disease.

Under normal circumstances, IL-10 acts as a chemical messenger between cells, helping the immune system regulate inflammation. However, certain antibodies can block its activity, effectively disabling one of the body's built-in safeguards against excessive immune responses. Without this protection, inflammation can persist and become difficult to control.

Hidden Antibodies Reveal a Cause of Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic conditions that affect approximately 500,000 people in the UK and millions more around the world.

Symptoms often first appear during adolescence or early adulthood, and patients may face lifelong medical challenges. Managing the disease can involve repeated hospital visits, medications that suppress immune activity, and sometimes surgery. Although treatments have improved, many people must try several different therapies without achieving lasting relief. This places a substantial burden on patients and creates significant costs for healthcare systems.

The researchers discovered that approximately 3.5% of patients with IBD had elevated levels of antibodies that neutralize IL-10. These antibodies were detected in people with both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, but not in healthy individuals.

Based on the prevalence of IBD in the UK, the researchers estimate that 15,000 to 20,000 patients nationwide could carry these harmful antibodies.

Scientists Solve a 30-Year Genetic Mystery

The investigation also revealed a strong association between the IL-10-blocking antibodies and a genetic variant called HLA-DRB1*01:03.

Scientists at Oxford first connected this genetic variant to a severe form of inflammatory bowel disease 30 years ago. However, the biological process linking the gene to the condition had remained unclear.

The new results help resolve that longstanding mystery. People who carry HLA-DRB1*01:03 are substantially more likely to develop antibodies that interfere with IL-10, providing an explanation for how this genetic risk factor can contribute to severe intestinal inflammation.

Professor Holm Uhlig, a pediatric gastroenterologist and Director of the Centre for Human Genetics at the University of Oxford's Nuffield Department of Medicine, was a senior author of the study.

"We've suspected an important role of interleukin 10 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease for decades. The study now provides clear evidence and contributes the missing link between a well-known genetic variant that had been linked to severe inflammatory bowel disease in the past and the very recently discovered autoimmunity to interleukin 10."

"Understanding what drives the inflammation, provides a clear explanation for disease in this group of people and opens the door to new treatments that target the autoantibodies themselves or cells that produce those autoantibodies."

How Earlier Discoveries Helped Explain Severe IBD

The findings build on more than a decade of research into rare inherited disorders that disrupt the body's ability to control inflammation.

Sophie Hambleton, Professor of Pediatrics and Immunology at Newcastle University, explained that studying these uncommon conditions provided important clues about the mechanisms involved in more widespread forms of IBD.

"This discovery shows how the study of rare, inherited disorders can shed new light on common conditions. The groundwork was laid over 10 years ago when genetic defects in IL-10 or its receptor were found in young children with severe IBD. Later, we realized that neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-10 were mimicking this effect in 2 little girls with colitis."

These earlier observations helped researchers recognize that antibodies blocking IL-10 could produce effects similar to inherited defects involving the same protein or its receptor. The latest study now establishes the importance of this mechanism in a larger group of patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

A Blood Test Could Lead to More Targeted IBD Treatments

Beyond explaining a previously mysterious cause of intestinal inflammation, the discovery could have important implications for patient care.

Researchers believe the results provide a foundation for developing a blood test that identifies people whose disease is associated with antibodies against IL-10. Such a test could help doctors recognize these patients earlier and select treatments that address the underlying immune malfunction.

Dr. Rainer Doffinger, a clinical immunologist at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, highlighted the potential benefits for both patients and healthcare systems.

"By identifying patients early and giving them targeted treatment, we could reduce reliance on expensive ongoing therapy and prevent complications. Even modest reductions in biologic treatment, admissions and surgery could translate into savings of many millions of pounds annually for the NHS, alongside the major benefits for patients through fewer interventions, improved quality of life or even durable remission."

Targeting the antibodies themselves, or the immune cells responsible for producing them, could offer a new treatment strategy for this particular group of patients. The approach could potentially reduce the need for repeated therapies, hospital admissions, and surgery while improving the chances of sustained disease control.

Professor Simon Travis, Professor of Clinical Gastroenterology at the University of Oxford and the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, emphasized the significance of identifying a specific biological cause of IBD.

"This is the most exciting discovery in a lifetime specialising in IBD. It means that we can now identify a group where we know what is causing the disease and that creates a real opportunity to change how we manage this disease."

The research marks an important advance toward personalized treatment for inflammatory bowel disease. Rather than relying primarily on symptoms to guide medical decisions, doctors may eventually be able to use biological testing to determine what is driving inflammation in individual patients and choose more appropriate therapies.

The study involved researchers from the Nuffield Department of Medicine at the University of Oxford, Newcastle University's Translational and Clinical Research Institute, and the Department of Immunology at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Funding was provided through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centres in Oxford, Cambridge, and Newcastle.

#5698. CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark

CVS Health plans to split pharmacy business from Aetna, Caremark" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The healthcare giant announced Wednesday morning that it would divide its business units into two companies. The first houses its retail pharmacies and Health 100 technology businesses, and will operate as CVS Pharmacy. The second includes Aetna, Caremark, Oak Street Health and Signify Health and will be referred to as CVS Health on an interim basis.

CVS said in the announcement that it expects the separation to be completed in the first half of 2028, subject to closing conditions, and until then, it will continue to operate jointly. The move will reverse CVS' historic acquisition of Aetna for $69 billion in 2018.

Current CVS CEO David Joyner will become chief executive of the new CVS Health, while Prem Shah, group president of CVS Health, will become the CEO of the new CVS Pharmacy unit.

The company said that the decision "follows a comprehensive strategic review" by its board of directors.

Joyner said during the company's earnings call Wednesday morning that the shift comes "from a position of strength" after multiple years of hard work at CVS to shift its strategic approach and drive improvement. That includes significant investments in technology across the enterprise, and an overhaul of its leadership team to drive needed change.

He said that the "environment around us is constantly changing" as the company pushes toward this new strategy.

"We can take this strategic action today because of our tremendous progress since 2024," Joyner said.

"We will be better positioned to address this changing environment as two strong independent healthcare leaders," he continued. "Following a thoughtful and deliberate strategic review by the board and senior management, we have a structure and plan that are built to win and represent the best path to create value over the long term."

During this process, the team has identified significant opportunities for greater integration between Aetna and Caremark and has leaned on those to support key strategic initiatives, like advancing value-based care, Joyner noted. However, the pharmacy business has generally "operated behind a firewall."

"It has always been an arm's length negotiation and structure, which again, just reinforces the fact that there are integration opportunities, but nothing that we cannot solve for with a commercial agreement," Joyner said.

While there are clear synergies that exist between the pharmacies and Caremark, those commercial deals can maintain what's working, he added.

"We don't need the integration in an operating structure," Joyner said. "We need to make sure that we're aligned around where we believe that there can be value creation and make sure that there's an appropriate commercial agreement in place to support that."

CVS' strategy over the past several years has been built on four key principles: delivering on best-in-class execution, rethinking the consumer experience, becoming a go-to partner and harnessing capabilities across the company.

Following the split, both companies will continue to lean on these concepts, CVS said. Each individual entity will also benefit from a more focused strategy and the ability to adapt more nimbly to its own unique goals and strategic needs.

The future CVS Pharmacy will continue to identify ways to expand the reach of its pharmacists and identify further partnerships across the healthcare spectrum, while CVS Health will adapt in new ways to serve its clients, the company said.

Joyner said the company will continue to be transparent about its progress during the separation process.

Shares in the company were up 3% pre-market as of about 7:30 a.m. ET. CVS also reported its Q3 earnings on Wednesday, posting $2.2 billion in profit and $108.4 billion in revenue for the quarter.

Joyner said on the earnings call that post-split, investors will own shares in both companies.
